title: Youngest Black professor at Cambridge resigns as university investigates allegations of plagiarism
description: A British sociologist who became famous as the youngest Black professor ever at the University of Cambridge has resigned after the university opened an investigation into “new information” about his a...
fullText:
LONDON (AP) — A British sociologist who became famous as the youngest Black professor ever at the University of Cambridge has resigned after the university opened an investigation into "new information" about his academic qualifications.

Professor Jason Arday, who was 37 when he became a Cambridge professor in 2023, announced his decision late Wednesday following weeks of allegations about plagiarism in his academic work and questions surrounding claims about his athletic and fundraising accomplishments.

"While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement," Arday said in a statement. "The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

The statement was distributed by the Good Law Project, a campaign group that has supported Arday since the criticism spilled into the media last month. An earlier letter circulated by the group and signed by more than two dozen academics and politicians described the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to undermine Arday and other Black people who hold "positions of influence."

Arday's appointment at Cambridge highlighted his personal story of overcoming dyslexia, developmental delays and autism that he said left him non-verbal until the age of 11 and illiterate until his late teens.

Questions about his qualifications were raised publicly last month by Nathan Cofnas, a one-time Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the university after his critique of diversity, equity and inclusion programs sparked widespread protests.

On July 24, the Times of London published an analysis of Arday's 2015 Ph.D. thesis highlighting what it said were multiple examples of passages that were "identical or near-identical" to an earlier paper written by another researcher.

The British media also raised questions about Arday's claims that he had raised 5.5 million pounds ($7.4 million) for charity through feats such as running 30 marathons in 35 days and 600 miles in six days.

Arday told the Guardian news website that the money was raised with the help of others over a 20-year period. He said non-disclosure agreements prevented him from naming the others.

Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.

That changed Wednesday when Cambridge opened its inquiry.

"The University of Cambridge has begun an investigation following new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments," the university said in a statement. "In order to ensure a fair process, we will not comment further until this has concluded."

The Times of London said Cambridge decided to investigate after it presented new evidence that some of Arday's research was "fabricated" and contained "impossible" evidence.

In an interview with the newspaper published last week, Arday denied plagiarism but admitted to some mistakes that he said were partly due to a lack of supervision when he was working on his doctorate.

Arday continued to defend himself in his resignation statement, saying his decision "should not be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship."

"Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me'" he said. "It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure."

title: ‘Is she even allowed to be doing this?’: Inside a federal judge’s side gig running a PR firm
description: Jennifer Mascott’s tenure at public affairs firm Adfero sparked questions around conflicts of interest and partisanship.
fullText:
A Trump-appointed federal appeals judge spent months running a Washington public affairs firm after being appointed to the bench last year, an arrangement that contributed to an exodus among the firm's staff and clients and only ended when the firm went out of business at the end of June.

Jennifer Mascott, a former conservative law professor who sits on the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals, was deeply involved in daily operations at the firm, Adfero, for at least six months after she was confirmed as a judge in October 2025, according to 14 former employees and clients granted anonymity to discuss internal details of the firm's final months.

Nine of the former employees said Mascott, who inherited her ownership stake in the firm from her late husband in 2023, worked at least once a week out of Adfero's office in Washington and oversaw the firm's staffing, business development efforts and client relations in between her full-time judicial duties in Wilmington and Philadelphia.

The firm was historically a nonpartisan business that did public relations and marketing work for companies and trade associations such as PhRMA and the National Retail Federation. In the final months of the business, Mascott brought on consultants with strong MAGA credentials, according to eight of the former employees and clients. Her leadership of the firm involved operational and strategic decisions: She required her signoff on marketing materials and suggested staff pitch the firm's services to health insurers after the loss of crucial clients like PhRMA.

The details of Mascott's involvement with the firm, which have not been previously reported, come amid a yearslong push by members of Congress and others in the legal community for stricter ethical requirements for judges. While judges are barred from engaging in business activities that could call their impartiality into question, they may maintain ownership of family businesses as long as they are not using the prestige of their judgeship to further the business or taking significant time away from their judicial duties.

Mascott said she adhered to legal and ethical requirements and ensured she was fully transparent with relevant authorities during her stewardship of Adfero. But her former employees and some of the firm's clients said the arrangement made them uncomfortable. And ultimately, the resulting loss of staff and clients led to the demise of the company after two decades in operation.

Mascott said she ran the firm as managing trustee, as requested by her late husband Jeff Mascott. Adfero was a third act for Jeff Mascott, who got his start working in House Republican offices and co-founded a constituent relationship management platform that was later acquired by FiscalNote. He founded Adfero 20 years ago and served as its CEO until a pancreatic cancer diagnosis in late 2022; he passed away in 2023.

Jennifer Mascott first took an active role in the management of Adfero at the beginning of 2025, when the second Trump administration began, according to seven former employees.

"Consistent with those fiduciary and legal and ethical duties, I endeavored to keep the company going while that was viable and also routinely consulted with long-time firm HR lawyers and other advisors and legal and ethical experts about how to comply with all requirements and how to evaluate whether the company should be wound down, sold, or otherwise entrusted to other firm leadership," she said in a statement to POLITICO.

Judicial ethics experts said Mascott's operation of the firm falls in a gray area, given its nature as a family business. The U.S. court system's code of conduct for judges generally allows continued participation in "a closely held family business," but warns such participation "may be prohibited if it takes too much time or involves misuse of judicial prestige or if the business is likely to come before the court on which the judge serves."

"If she is logging time there and it has the potential to interfere with her judicial duties, that is a no-go," said Charles Geyh, a law professor at the Indiana University Mauer School of Law who studies judicial ethics.

The nature of Adfero's work — the firm's website boasts examples of its marketing campaigns designed to "influence elected officials" — makes Mascott's situation unique, said retired federal judge Nancy Gertner, an appointee of President Bill Clinton who has called for Supreme Court justices to adopt the same code of ethics that binds lower court judges like Mascott.

"It's not like she's making widgets," she said. "A company that she controls is sending out a message that she could never send out directly."

Mascott told staffers who questioned the arrangement that her management posed no problem as long as she recused herself from matters involving the firm, its clients or potential clients, according to three of the former employees. The explanation did little to assuage their concerns.

"On one hand, maybe the owner of the company should be involved, but on the other hand she's a judge," said one former employee. "People asked me 'Is this legal?' I don't know. 'Is this ethical?' Certainly not."

One former client pointed to Mascott's unusual arrangement as one reason they sought services elsewhere.

"She came in and was running the organization while being a federal judge, and it got very weird," said the former client. "All of a sudden, staff started leaving, and we saw that as an inflection point that it was time to move on."

Mascott had been a well-known figure in Washington's conservative legal circles long before Trump nominated her to the appeals court. A former clerk for then-D.C. Circuit Judge Brett Kavanaugh and Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas, Mascott later worked in the Justice Department during Trump's first term and the White House counsel's office during his second. Since her confirmation, she's heard appeals spanning immigration, criminal law, civil rights, employment and commercial disputes alongside Trump ally Emil Bove on the 3rd Circuit — all while attempting to keep Adfero afloat.

Throughout her vetting and confirmation process, she remained active on social media and made public appearances, including one with Thomas — unusual practices for judicial nominees, who typically refrain from public statements while they are being evaluated by the Senate. Delaware Democratic Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester and Chris Coons panned her lack of relevant experience when Trump tapped her for the Delaware-based seat.

"She has never been a judge of any kind, yet she is nominated to one of the highest judicial posts in the country," Rochester and Coons said of Mascott in a July 2025 statement. "As far as we know, her relationship to Delaware is confined to a vacation beach house she sometimes visits in our state."

Mascott defended her legal experience during her September 2025 confirmation hearing, noting that she had filed dozens of appellate briefs around the country, including in the 3rd Circuit, and pledged to base her chambers in Wilmington, if confirmed.

Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) introduced Mascott at her confirmation hearing where he praised her legal scholarship, calling her "the perfect candidate for federal judge." Mascott — a member of the Federalist Society since 2006 — has testified against legislation to strengthen ethics guardrails for Supreme Court justices and publicly defended the court's rulings on presidential immunity and abortion.

Mascott disclosed her ownership of Adfero during the confirmation process, writing in documents submitted to the Senate Judiciary Committee that her "late husband's estate contains a public affairs firm" and pledging to recuse herself from any matter involving Adfero or its clients.

Although employees felt sympathy for the widow of their beloved former boss, they swiftly began to chafe at Mascott's leadership.

"It was never fully addressed out in the open, but people definitely brought it up in their one-on-ones with their managers," said a second former employee. "There were whispers of, 'Is she even allowed to be doing this?'"

In February 2025, an Adfero account executive published an op-ed in PR Week on the importance of diversity, equity and inclusion in public relations. Adfero promoted the op-ed on its social media accounts until Mascott had the posts removed, according to four former employees. Mascott sent the staffer flowers congratulating her on the op-ed, but afterwards started requiring her approval on the firm's marketing materials.

After she was confirmed as a judge, one of Mascott's first actions at Adfero was removing Darren Scher, who led the firm immediately after Jeff Mascott's death, and Lauren Tyler, the firm's chief of staff. "That was a very shocking thing," said the first former employee regarding the October 2025 announcement during a staff meeting. "I didn't think it was real at first."

Eight former employees described Scher and Tyler's abrupt departure as a turning point for the firm, with several saying resignations began to pile up in the ensuing months. Scher and Tyler did not respond to requests for comment.

The shift within the firm was a stark contrast for its longtime employees. Under the late Jeff Mascott, the firm had racked up accolades that still appear on Adfero's website: a "Top Place to Work in PR" mention by PR Week and finalist for "Boutique PR Firm of the Year." Jeff Mascott was also included in PR Week's "40 Under 40" list in 2008.

"Toward the beginning of spring, I just remember coming back from weekends and finding stacks of goodbye cards from coworkers that had already left — and these are people I'd work with on Friday," said a third former staffer. "Departures just became really frequent and happened really quietly and quickly."

Remaining staff at the firm were stretched thin as departures picked up. In January, Adfero's CEO Steve Lombardo submitted his resignation, less than a year after joining the firm. He declined to comment.

"At one point, about a year ago, we were getting one resignation a month," said the second former employee. "But then it quickly turned into one person a week, around January, and then it quickly turned into one person a day."

Clients began taking note. One by one, several high-profile clients who had been with the firm for years jumped ship. The loss of one of those clients, PhRMA, hurt particularly hard.

The pharmaceutical industry trade group told Adfero in January this year that it would not renew its seven-figure contract with the firm, six former employees said. But Jennifer Mascott was undeterred, according to four of the former employees, describing the loss of the anchor client as an opportunity to pursue new business among health insurers, whose policy goals are generally opposed to the pharmaceutical industry lobby. PhRMA declined to comment.

Two former clients told POLITICO they decided to end their work with Adfero because nearly their entire account teams had left the firm. On multiple occasions, firm clients saw their entire account teams resign but were not told until the last minute due to a directive from Mascott that firm departures not be announced until just before a staffer's final day, four former employees and one client said.

As staff left, Mascott brought on consultants with deep ties to the GOP to help fill the gaps: Luke Ball — a former Trump campaign operative and frequent guest on Fox News who worked for then-Reps. Matt Gaetz (R-Fla.) and Madison Cawthorn (R-N.C.) — and Ben Stout, a former deputy chief of staff for Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.). At least two clients declined to renew their contracts with Adfero in part because they felt Mascott was taking the firm in a more partisan direction, according to two former clients.

"We've always been bipartisan or nonpartisan, and that was sincerely very, very true," said the second former employee. "And then there was a shift with the consultants that she hired. The politics-leaning was just very blatant, and that was a departure from what people were used to."

Ball declined to comment, and Stout did not respond to a request for comment.

"I feel confident speaking on behalf of my former coworkers on this: We all loved working there when it was in its prime," a fourth former employee said. "It was just tough to see it all play out the way it ended up playing out."

title: America’s Third Red Scare
description: Pietro A....
fullText:
Trump and the revival of “red-hunting” demagoguery.

A “communist assault” on the US, you say?

A “red menace” sweeping American workplaces and washrooms?

“Socialist subterfuge” from Chicago to Cleveland?

Such talking points might sound like echoes from a seemingly distant past, from the dark days of the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), when even the slightest accusation of communism was enough to destroy one’s life and career. Yet in 2026 President Trump, in his characteristically demagogic style, has sought to dust off such “red” rhetoric and employ it for a new assault against free speech and civil liberties, in advance of a potentially disastrous midterm election. Taking a page from the old playbook of Joe McCarthy, Trump has spared no expense in painting his opponents with the red brush of communism. “Communism’s easy to sell,” Trump declared at the NATO summit in Turkey last month. “I would be the greatest communist in history; I’d be right up there with Lenin,” he boasted, adding that communism has “proven to be a disaster” for “thousands of years.” Never mind that The Communist Manifesto was only published in 1848.

Trump’s buffoonish bravado would seem the stuff of unimaginative comedy were it not to have such deleterious implications for First Amendment rights. The main targets of the president’s fury are New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and his allies in the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). A string of recent electoral victories of progressives over establishment Democrats have unnerved the powers that be in both parties. Donald Trump and the GOP have particular reasons to be jittery, amid rising economic turbulence, a historically unpopular war against Iran, and the ongoing genocide in Gaza. Indeed, a perfect storm seems to be brewing for the president in November. In this context, the reliance on HUAC talking points not only serves as a natural weapon in Trump’s tool kit for debasing democracy, but also as a kind of “salute” to the memory of his mentor, the odious Roy Cohn, a direct link to the McCarthyite legacy of intimidation, lies, and obfuscation.

To be sure, the communist charges leveled against Mamdani are nothing new in the context of the GOP’s larger weaponization of all forms of socialism. However, such accusations have lost their bite in recent years, as more and more Americans turn toward democratic socialism in response to fast-growing wealth inequality, forever wars, and corporate influence on Capitol Hill. In fact, Mayor Mamdani’s impressive record in New York—following in the footsteps of Fiorello La Guardia—only highlights the success of progressive alternatives in American politics. Thus, the revival of explicitly McCarthyite talking points can only be read as a desperate move, a form of fatuous fearmongering from a failing presidency. The situation is apparently desperate enough that even Trump’s “court liberal,” the comedian Bill Maher, has chimed in to castigate Mamdani as a “straight-up communist.”

However, the deployment of “red-hunting” tactics does not stop at mere electioneering. It also serves as a means of attacking civil liberties and silencing domestic critics of the Trump administration. Most recently, one of those critics, the independent progressive journalist Max Blumenthal, in violation of his First and Fourth Amendment rights, had two of his smartphones confiscated by US Customs and Border Protection without any explanation. Blumenthal was returning to the US from Iran, where he covered not only the funeral of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei but also the impact of Trump’s criminal war against the Iranian people. For this alone, Laura Loomer, the looniest of Trump’s neocon nuts, took to Twitter to accuse Blumenthal of being “one of the leading communist voices in America.” The hope of Loomer and her fellow Trumpian loonies is to criminalize dissent and silence all critical reporting on the Iran war and American imperialism more generally. For his part, Blumenthal and the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC) have fought back, with the ADC issuing a motion calling on the government to immediately return the two seized smartphones. The government complied shortly afterward.

The administration’s attacks on communism are also tied to the president’s focus on giving a new lease on life to American imperialism in the Western Hemisphere. Following the coup in Venezuela and the illegal abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, Trump’s neocon acolytes have become giddy at the prospect of achieving “regime change on the cheap.” Empowered by their “success,” they have now set their sights squarely on Cuba. In his first term, Trump already signaled an interest in reviving American imperialist designs on the island nation—from his decision to cancel Obama-era rapprochement to declaring Havana a “state sponsor of terrorism.” In the push for a coup against “red Cuba,” Trump’s secretary of state, Marco Rubio—the son of Cuban immigrants who fled before the 1959 revolution—has assumed an especially vocal role. By all accounts, it was Rubio who was the chief architect of the aggressive starvation blockade that is now besieging the beleaguered island.

Particularly noteworthy in the context of the rising Third Red Scare have been Rubio’s efforts to directly tie Trump’s regime-change fantasies with the president’s campaign to stifle dissent at home. Baselessly branding Havana a sponsor of what Rubio deems “Far Left Terrorism (FLT),” the secretary of state has issued a 100-page report praising the “harsh government crackdowns” of the McCarthy era and calling for a new wave of repressions against a slew of progressive and anti-war American organizations and individuals. From the DSA, to Code Pink, to even Ben & Jerry’s ice cream, nobody is safe from Little Marco’s “crusade” against the “commies” and other “fellow travelers.”

Yet, if history is any indication, Trump’s “New Red Scare,” much like Joe McCarthy’s, will fall flat on its face. If McCarthy’s downfall was secured by a Senate censure, supported by President Eisenhower, then Trump’s downfall will be secured by the fallout from America’s coming trials and tribulations. Truly, as the Iran war hobbles on and the global economy shows signs of serious strain, it is clear that Trump and his market manipulations can no longer disguise the hard reality that now faces the nation.

title: Collaborating With the MAHA Movement Is a Terrible Idea
description: Gregg...
fullText:
Some pundits are pushing a strategic alliance with parts of RFK Jr.’s base. Here’s why they’re wrong.

We’ve now had a year and a half to see what the “Make America Health Again” movement has wrought. Under the leadership of Robert F. Kennedy Jr., we’ve seen a full-scale attack on vaccination in the United States and the decimation of agencies like the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the National Institutes of Health, among many others. American public health and biomedical research are in free fall—and it’s all hazardous to your well-being. And MAHA and MAGA, despite bumps in the road, are partners in an authoritarian mission to put American health and lives under the thumb of Donald Trump and his henchmen hiding in the shadows, from Russell Vought to Jay Bhattacharya and Dr. Oz.

Yet, despite the people hurt by the administration’s policies, there are always others ready to make excuses for people in power. At the beginning of President Trump’s term, there were those who were in the mode of “wait, hear me out, RFK Jr. has some good ideas on what is wrong with health in America.” This logic depended on cherry-picking a few items on the MAHA agenda—on processed food or pharmaceutical advertising, for instance—while downplaying the very real dangers RFK Jr. posed overall. While these people may have seen themselves as bridge-builders to the new administration, they were really just offering up their own personal and professional credibility to people who didn’t give a damn what they thought. I still can’t fathom why they would do so.

All these months later, those voices have largely gone silent. Apparently, playing footsie with RFK Jr. is not what it used to be. However, what has persisted are those commentators who want to partake in another game of “just pick the cyclospora out of your salad.”

This time, rather than seeingm RFK Jr. as a possible partner, these individuals are seeking to separate MAHA supporters from those who lead the movement. Their pitch: The rank and file of MAHA are not all anti-vaxxers. They have real concerns about pesticides, ultra-processed foods, and the failure of the American healthcare system. You cannot lump them in with RFK Jr. and his ilk—these regular MAHA folks are real people we can work with.

The first problem with this argument is that there are many ways to tackle these issues that don’t involve cozying up to the MAHA faithful. There is an entire environmental movement addressing pesticides, many people addressing the lack of healthy food for millions of Americans, and hundreds of groups pushing for healthcare reform. For the rank and file, the decision to remain affiliated with MAHA and its pernicious politics is a choice. You may have come for the raw milk and beef tallow, but if you stay for the eugenics and outright racism built into the MAHA agenda, these pundits should at least ask why this is so. (What’s more, this country’s political leaders usually promote policies that make their supporters’ day-to-day lives more difficult. Why stay in what is an abusive political relationship?)

Another problem is that the image of MAHA as a broadly bipartisan movement is just not true. In fact, political affiliation is the strongest predictor of identification with MAHA; a Kaiser Family Foundation/Washington Post poll taken last fall found approximately “six in ten (62%) Republican parents identify[ing] with the movement, rising to eight in ten (81%) among Republicans who support the Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement.” The numbers for Democratic parents identifying with MAHA are much lower at 17 percent and among independents down to about a third.

But none of these questions matter to the MAHA-curious. In fact, for them it’s not MAHA that’s the problem; it’s public health. It’s true that trust in many civic and governmental institutions has been in decline across the board for over a decade. Public health is no exception, and the Covid pandemic did not help. But there is a profound ignorance of history that resides in these arguments. Naomi Oreskes and Erik Conway, in their book Merchants of Doubt, have described the long-standing campaign to undermine trust in public health and scientific institutions on topics as diverse as tobacco, global warming, and pesticides. During Covid, new merchants of doubt were out sowing discord and anger, often funded by far-right foundations, as well-documented by Walker Bragman and Alex Kotch. At the very least, some acknowledgement that trust can be actively undermined as a political strategy needs to be confronted by these commentators, which they are often not willing to do. They pass over the conservative actors and media ecosystem at work in fueling this crisis.

Improving public health depends on building a big tent. But it is an odd strategy indeed to always look rightward for allies and ignore those who are being hurt most by this administration’s policies—to eschew solidarity with those most in need of someone to care about them and their plight. To build your liberal brand on fetishization of conservative voices is a now well-worn and satirized trope (e.g., the New York Times Pitchbot’s “In this Ohio diner…” series). But in the context of these commentaries on public health, whom you seek out also tells you who matters, and whom you’re willing to leave behind.

A broad-based coalition for public health can be built, but if your starting place is kicking back a cup of coffee in the Ohio diner with MAHA influencers, rather than with the miners in Belmont County dying of black lung disease while the feds block new silica protection rules; or with the families living in food deserts in the Milo-Grogan and Linden communities in Columbus while President Trump axed a probe into price-fixing and collusion between this country’s biggest food company and its biggest grocer; or some of the hundreds of thousands of Ohioans about to lose Medicaid coverage under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, I’d repeat the words of Florence Reese, who sang in 1931 during the Harlan County, Kentucky miners’ strike: “Which side are you on?”

There are always grifters and opportunists ready to seize the moment, and the false populism of RFK Jr. and Donald Trump and the false tribune-of-the-people liberalism of MAHA’s fellow travelers strangely connect in a disinterest in the millions upon millions who will suffer from this administration’s policies. And yes, I think there are also those who, in good faith, see those among the MAHA rank and file as worthy of our concern. I do too. Health is a human right, and it belongs to all of us. But a new collaborationist politics is sprouting up which excuses too much and pretends that the world of MAHA is something other than it is: a movement built to destroy and built on lies by its founders.

If we want to build trust, we can start by telling the truth. To MAHA supporters, we can say in all honesty and with kindness and patience: The people you follow, the movement you are part of, is a con. Those who would redirect you to see public health as “the problem” are leading you astray as well. In the end, MAHA and its not-you-it’s-me mirror image of an illegitimate, untrustworthy conception of public health are just leading us down rabbit holes, away from the core problems we face today.

If you want to strike at the root of what ails all of us, stop and look at the politicians and their billionaire allies who have enriched themselves at our expense, gutting the programs that provide protection from health threats across the board, slashing programs that ensure healthcare for millions, leading many Americans to an early grave. This great unraveling is happening right before your eyes, and things are about to get a lot, lot worse. There is an epic political struggle brewing right now, and distraction is something we cannot afford in this existential moment, whether it is from a Kennedy or the pied pipers of the podcasts.

title: Swansea sign Scotland striker Stewart
description: Swansea City sign free agent Ross Stewart on a three-year deal following the Scotland striker's departure from Southampton.
fullText:
Swansea City have signed free agent Ross Stewart following the Scotland striker's departure from Southampton.

Stewart has penned a three-year deal at the Swansea.com Stadium having left the Saints in June after failing to agree a new contract.

The 30-year-old's arrival may be viewed as a move which casts further doubt over Zan Vipotnik's Swansea future, with the Slovenia international expected to attract interest in this transfer window after finishing last season as the Championship's top scorer.

Stewart - part of Scotland's squad at this summer's World Cup - has scored goals at Championship level for both Southampton and Sunderland and is seen as "an experienced and proven performer" at this level by Vitor Matos.

"In our conversations he has made clear his hunger and desire to be an important senior figure and leader in our dressing room," said the Swans' head coach.

"His goalscoring record shows he is someone who relishes responsibility and we look forward to getting down to work with him and settling him into the group."

Stewart scored 11 times in 33 games for Southampton last season, his best at St Mary's Stadium after injury issues restricted him to only 17 appearances across the previous two campaigns.

He has played four times for Scotland, including a substitute appearance against Morocco at this summer's World Cup.

Swansea have sold Liam Cullen to Leicester City this summer and could also allow Bobby Wales to depart on loan, meaning Stewart joins Vipotnik and Adam Idah as the forward options in Matos' squad.

Foundations now in place at Swansea - Gorringe

Stewart's remarkable rise from Scottish juniors to World Cup

Latest Swansea City news, analysis and fan views

Stewart missed a hefty chunk of the 2025-26 season because of a hamstring injury but was still productive when available, managing nine goals and two assists in his 27 league appearances last term.

He also scored two goals in Southampton's run to the semi-finals of the FA Cup, including the opener in their quarter-final victory over Arsenal.

Stewart had stints with Ardeer Thistle and Kilwinning Rangers as a youngster before joining Albion Rovers in 2016.

The Irvine-born player then played for St Mirren, Alloa Athletic and Ross County - where he won the 2018-19 Scottish Championship and Scottish Challenge Cup - before joining Sunderland in 2021.

Stewart was prolific with the Black Cats, scoring 40 goals in 81 appearances to help the club win the EFL Trophy in 2021 and gain promotion to the Championship a year later.

His form at the Stadium of Light earned him a move to Southampton in 2023, where he scored a total of 12 goals in 50 appearances.

"We are delighted that Ross has joined Swansea City, he brings a wealth of experience on and off the pitch," said the Welsh club's sporting director Ben Stevens.

"His performances last season in the Championship were a standout, and it earned him a deserved place in Scotland's World Cup squad. We are very excited to see Ross in a Swansea shirt."

Stewart becomes Swansea's sixth permanent signing of the summer after Moussa Yeo, Elijah Just, Joseph Opoku, Stephen Welsh and Leo Walta, who had been on loan last season.

They have also signed Benfica left-back Tiago Parente on loan.

Valencia's Andre Almeida and another midfielder, Ousseynou Fall Seck of Danish side Randers, are also on the Swans' list of targets.

title: London submits bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships
description: London submits its final bid to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships, with the London Stadium, built for the 2012 Olympics, the proposed venue.
fullText:
London has submitted its final bid to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships.

Athletic Ventures – a body made up of UK Athletics, London Marathon Events, and the Great Run Company – is behind the move to bring the biennial event to the capital and confirmed the final documents have been submitted to World Athletics.

London Stadium, built for the 2012 Olympics and used for the London Diamond League meeting for the past four years, is the proposed host venue.

The host city for the 2029 edition will be confirmed in September.

A feasibility study conducted prior to April 2025, when London's intention to bid was announced, said the competition could bring a £400m benefit to the economy, with the UK government confirming its support for the bid in July 2025.

Championship football team West Ham United, who play their home games at the London Stadium, have also offered their support for the bid.

Hodgkinson & Asher-Smith in GB squad for Europeans

London previously hosted the World Championship in 2017, while Birmingham will host the European Championships this August.

Great Run Company CEO Paul Foster hailed London as "the world's number one sporting city" while UK Athletics CEO Jack Buckner emphasised the importance of the event in the UK's "Olympic legacy".

Buckner said: "Bidding to hold the World Athletics Championships in the London Stadium, the showpiece of London 2012, was always at the centre of the UK's Olympic legacy plans.

"We are very grateful to the government, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, the Mayor of London, and UK sport for their fantastic support for this bid.

"We're delighted that we have reached agreement with the London Stadium and West Ham United for the use of the London Stadium and our sincere thanks for their commitment in making this happen."

In a statement, West Ham confirmed they are working with London Stadium LLP and Athletics Ventures to support the delivery of the Championships, with a "number of new initiatives that will enhance the stadium and matchday experience for supporters" forming part of the agreement.

The potential impact on their 2029-30 campaign if London's bid is successful is yet to be confirmed.

title: MotoGP extends British Grand Prix through to 2028
description: The British Grand Prix will remain on the MotoGP World Championship calendar until at least 2028 as Silverstone extends its partnership with MotoGP.
fullText:
The British Grand Prix will remain on the MotoGP World Championship calendar until at least 2028.

MotoGP has extended its partnership with Silverstone, which hosts the race, to cover the 2027 and 2028 seasons.

The British Grand Prix returned to Silverstone after a 24-year absence in 2010, having previously been held at Donington Park.

This year's race will take place on Sunday, 9 August – the 12th of 22 races in the 2026 calendar.

Italy's Marco Bezzecchi, currently fourth in the MotoGP standings, won at Silverstone last season.

Marquez continues Sachsenring dominance

Silverstone also hosts Formula 1 and the European Le Mans Series, and will return to the FIA World Endurance Championship schedule in 2027.

"This extension underscores our commitment to two-wheel racing," said CEO of Silverstone, Stuart Pringle.

"This renewed partnership secures our place as the undisputed home of elite international racing."

Carmelo Ezpeleta, CEO of MotoGP Group, added: "The UK has a rich motorcycle racing heritage and remains one of the most important markets for MotoGP.

"Silverstone provides a fantastic stage for MotoGP, 11 different winners in the last 11 Grands Prix hosted at the circuit is a testament to the quality, competitiveness and unpredictability of racing at the circuit."

title: Bournemouth sign Spanish right-back Juanlu
description: Bournemouth announce the signing of right-back Juanlu Sanchez from Spanish club Sevilla in a deal worth up to £11.1m.
fullText:
Bournemouth have announced the signing of right-back Juanlu Sanchez from Spanish club Sevilla in a deal worth up to £11.1m.

The 22-year-old arrives at the Cherries with more than 100 senior appearances after breaking into the Sevilla first team, and has played in the Champions League, Uefa Super Cup and La Liga.

The Spaniard is also an Olympic gold medallist with Spain in 2024, where he scored the match-winning goal in the semi-final against Morocco before helping his country beat France in the final.

"I am very happy, both for me and for my family. We had a lot of desire to come here and finally I can say that I am a player of Bournemouth," Juanlu told the club.

Juanlu will cost an initial £9.4m, with a further £1.7m in add-ons, BBC Sport believes.

Speaking on Juanlu's arrival, the Cherries' president of football operations, Tiago Pinto, said: "Juanlu has an excellent level of experience at just 22, and we're really pleased to add him to Marco's squad.

"With Sevilla, he has shown his qualities domestically and in European competitions, so we know of his ability to compete at the top level consistently.

"He is young still and hungry for more, so adds further invaluable characteristics to the squad ahead of the upcoming season.

"We're really looking forward to seeing how he continues to progress here with us and for how he will develop with Marco and the team."

Juanlu is the Cherries' third signing of the summer after the arrivals of Antonio Silva from Benfica for £25.7m and striker Alvaro Rodriguez from Elche - also for £25.7m - earlier in the transfer window.

Bournemouth boss Marco Rose is now looking for a number two goalkeeper capable of challenging Djordje Petrovic as Bournemouth continue pre-season before a historic campaign in which they will compete in the Europa League for the first time.

Sevilla have shown an interest in striker Enes Unal, who Bournemouth are keen to sell. However, the Turkey international also has options in Turkey and Saudi Arabia as he looks to secure a move this summer.

Star trio Eli Junior Kroupi, Rayan and Alex Scott are not for sale, according to senior sources at the Vitality Stadium.

title: 114 days and counting - how damaging is Alcaraz's wrist injury?
description: BBC Sport analyses Carlos Alcaraz's ongoing absence from tennis and why wrist injuries are so difficult to manage.
fullText:
When Carlos Alcaraz walked off the court at Rod Laver Arena in January, he was on top of the world.

At 22, he had just completed the career Grand Slam, beating all-time great Novak Djokovic in the Australian Open final to claim his seventh major title.

A few months earlier he had decimated his rival Jannik Sinner in the US Open final in what was one of most the impressive performances of his illustrious career to date.

But the Spaniard has now missed the French Open and Wimbledon, going 114 days without playing a competitive match due to a wrist injury he suffered in April.

After returning to training, he has now withdrawn from the upcoming Cincinnati Open, and with the US Open less than a month away, Alcaraz's ability to defend his title is in serious doubt.

So, why exactly is Alcaraz's injury proving so troublesome, and how problematic can wrist issues be for tennis players in the long run?

Alcaraz has been suffering from tenosynovitis - a painful inflammation of the fluid-filled sheath that surrounds the tendon on the inside of the wrist.

Tenosynovitis is typically caused by repetitive movements like gripping and swinging a tennis racket, and can lead to swelling and ongoing tenderness.

Minor cases can take weeks to recover, mostly managed by rest, but more severe issues can require significant physiotherapy and potentially even surgery, with recovery taking up to a year.

Alcaraz has not undergone surgery, but his latest withdrawal will take him to over four months out injured, and for a portion of that he was unable to use a racquet at all.

Wrist injuries are particularly worrisome for tennis players. The joint plays a key role in every contact between the racquet and ball - the way the wrist rolls through a shot helps generate power, and its dexterity is vital for delicate touches like drop shots, which are a key part of Alcaraz's all-court game.

The lack of muscle surrounding the bones and tendons in the wrists also makes rebuilding strength difficult, meaning the length of absences can be difficult to predict.

"They're much tougher injuries," 1996 Wimbledon champion Richard Krajicek told Tennis365.

"It's really difficult to reset when you start playing again [after this type injury]. You need to go step by step.

"It's not as clear-cut as tearing the ligaments in your ankle, which [you know takes] three or four months and then you can play again."

As tennis has become quicker, with the majority of players on both tours hitting hard from the baseline and using a double-handed backhand, the ability to generate power and top-spin has become even more important, increasing the strain on players' wrists.

Grand Slam winners Dominic Thiem and Juan Martin del Potro both suffered recurring wrist injuries throughout their careers.

"Wrist injuries are becoming more significant in the game," says James Ross, a physiotherapist who works with players at Grand Slams and other tournaments.

"A big factor is technological improvements - racquets and strings are better, so the ball is coming at you with more force and you've got to be able to absorb that.

"Tennis players also have a more gruelling schedule than ever before, putting more strain on the joints, and the balls are inconsistent between tournaments - changes like that mean the body has to adapt and that presents an injury risk."

Alcaraz won his last match against a qualifier in the opening round of the Barcelona Open, but was in visible discomfort and withdrew before his next match.

A competitive return is still a few weeks off at least, however, meaning he will at best be carrying almost five months' worth of rust into the US Open if he plays.

But with wrist injuries in tennis, waiting longer can help prevent the problem recurring.

"The biggest risk of injury is a previous injury - if you have had it once, you are more likely to have it in the future," Ross adds.

"If a player can get back over a period of a few months and they don't have a reoccurrence, generally they will be OK.

"But some things can become chronic and the pressure of the sport to come back, earn money by playing, and keep your ranking points, is a risk."

One of the key challenges of a wrist injury is psychological - once a player has suffered a painful injury in the joint that controls so much of their technique, it can be difficult to fully trust it again.

"Wrists aren't easy", said Sir Andy Murray, having suffered injuries in both wrists in his early 20s.

"When the ball is low you know you really have to use your wrist to get the ball up and down, or when the ball is coming fast and quite high you need to use your wrist a lot to bring the ball down.

"It's difficult when you try to come back [from a wrist injury], because the pain that you feel when you initially hurt it, mentally it's very difficult to let go of."

Before his injury, Alcaraz had been performing at an extremely impressive average of two Grand Slam titles per year. Continuing at that pace would have him level with Novak Djokovic's record of 24 by 2034, when he will be only 31.

Alcaraz will hope to return to top form as soon as he is back on court, but reaching the same level of performance following a wrist injury isn't easy.

"The wrist doesn't get great blood supply and it doesn't heal very quickly," says Ross. "It takes real time to build strength in it and the management is very complex.

"Restoring confidence is down to how rehab goes - you can feel amazing and then get a setback, and it's how you deal with that.

"We also treat injuries as windows of opportunity - you might not be able to hit a tennis ball right now, but let's work on your cardiovascular fitness, work on the core and lower body, or see how you mentally decompress and cope with having a holiday.

"You really have to keep the player motivated."

title: Bangor's Arthurs served cocaine use ban last year
description: Bangor striker Ben Arthurs is free to play in his club's first game of the 2026-27 Irish Premiership season having completed a three-month ban anti-doping ban.
fullText:
Bangor striker Ben Arthurs has completed a three-month ban after testing positive for cocaine following an Irish Premiership game in March.

The 28-year-old was subject to an anti-doping test after his side faced Glentoran on 10 March and a statement from UK Anti-Doping [UKAD] on Thursday said Arthurs admitted to "ingesting cocaine for recreational purposes within a social setting".

Under UKAD rules, athletes can be issued reduced three-month suspensions "if they can establish that they used the substance out-of-competition and in a context unrelated to sport performance".

An independent expert concluded that the use of the drug "most likely" took place before the day of the game, which Glentoran won 4-0.

The 28-year-old was suspended by Bangor in April and at the time it was said the Seasiders were "unable to provide further details" while an investigation took place.

With Arthurs' having been issued with a provisional suspension on 7 April, his ban has been served and, having already returned to pre-season training, he is eligible to face Cliftonville at Clandeboye Park when Lee Feeney's side begin their 2026-27 Irish Premiership campaign on 15 August.

It will be Arthurs' ninth season at the club where he is the second top goalscorer in their history.

Doping control was introduced in the Irish Premiership and Women's Premiership in 2024 in a move joint-funded by the Irish Football Association [IFA] and Northern Ireland Football League [NIFL].

BBC NI approached the IFA and NIFL for comment.

title: Ex-Brazil forward Pato's consortium to take over Northampton
description: Former AC Milan and Brazil forward Alexandre Pato is a member of a consortium which is set to buy a majority stake in League Two club Northampton Town, BBC Sport understands.
fullText:
A consortium including former AC Milan, Chelsea and Brazil forward Alexandre Pato is set to buy a majority stake in League Two club Northampton Town, BBC Sport understands.

Sports Alpha Capital was in discussions about taking over Colchester United earlier this year but decided to pull out of a potential deal following initial talks.

It is understood Pato is involved with the consortium but is not fronting it.

The 36-year-old retired from playing last year. He is best known for his five-and-a-half-year spell at AC Milan where he scored 63 goals in 150 matches and won the Serie A title in the 2010-11 season.

He spent the second half of the 2015-16 season on loan at Chelsea from Corinthians and scored on his debut from the penalty spot in a 4-0 win at Aston Villa.

The news comes after Northampton chairman Kelvin Thomas confirmed last month that a "well-funded" group's proposed investment had been "pretty much agreed".

The Cobblers suffered relegation to the fourth tier last season, finishing bottom of the League One table.

In April, the club announced a pre-tax loss just short of £3m with Thomas previously saying that the proposed investment would make the club debt-free.

Northampton appointed Chris Hogg as their manager in May and have so far brought in seven new players in the transfer window, including striker Matty Warhurst from Manchester City and midfielder Connor Lemonheigh-Evans from MK Dons.

title: Argentina mark World Cup win over England with National Football Teams Day
description: The Argentine Football Association announces 15 July as National Football Teams Day to mark Argentina's 2026 World Cup semi-final victory over England.
fullText:
The Argentine Football Association, external has announced 15 July will be 'National Football Teams Day' to mark Argentina's 2026 World Cup semi-final victory over England on that date.

Bidding for their first World Cup final since 1966, England took the lead in a tense affair in Atlanta through a 55th-minute Anthony Gordon finish.

But with Thomas Tuchel's side sitting deep, Argentina struck in the 85th and 92nd minutes to break English hearts and claim a 2-1 win.

The victory came 40 years after Argentina's previous big World Cup win over England in the controversial quarter-final victory at the 1986 tournament.

After Argentina's latest win the political tensions surrounding the fixture were fuelled as some of their players celebrated while holding a banner reading "Las Malvinas son Argentinas", which translates as "The Falklands are Argentine".

The Falklands, a British Overseas Territory in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between the UK and Argentina.

Argentina, ruled at the time by a military junta led by General Leopoldo Galtieri, invaded the islands, situated 300 miles off Argentina's east coast, in 1982.

The conflict, which lasted for 74 days between April and June 1982, led to the deaths of 655 Argentine and 255 British servicemen. Three people from the islands also died.

In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of Falkland Islanders voted to remain a UK territory.

Argentina went on to lose 1-0 to Spain in the 2026 final, while England beat France 6-4 to claim third place.

title: Hampshire and England bowler Turner retires aged 25
description: Hampshire and England fast bowler John Turner retires from cricket aged 25 after more than a year out injured.
fullText:
Hampshire and England fast bowler John Turner has retired from cricket because of persistent injuries.

The 25-year-old has not played for his county since last summer due to a stress fracture in his back.

Turner, who was born in South Africa, represented England in two one-day internationals and two T20 games at the end of 2024 during their tour of the West Indies.

He was selected in the England T20 squad the year before for their series against New Zealand, but was then ruled out through injury.

"This has been one of the hardest decisions I've had to make," Turner said.

Why Turner could be England's McGrath

"The stress fracture, which has sidelined me for over a year, as well as my injury record, naturally made me think of my future both as a cricketer and away from the game, and subsequently, I decided now was the right time to pursue my next challenge."

Turner made his debut for Hampshire in 2021, claiming former England captain Alastair Cook as his first wicket in a One-Day Cup match.

In total, Turner played 51 matches for Hampshire across all formats, taking 97 wickets.

During the T20 Blast in 2023 he claimed 21 wickets at an average of 11.76 and an economy of 6.67 - stats that earned him his first England call-up, months after playing for England Lions in New Zealand.

He also played for Trent Rockets in The Hundred and alongside cricket completed his studies for an economics degree.

"It was always my dream to play professional and international cricket, and doing so for Hampshire and England has been nothing short of living out those same childhood dreams," Turner added.

Hampshire director of cricket Giles White said Turner had been a "huge part" of the club's success over the past five years.

"John is an exceptionally talented player, and all of Hampshire Cricket is saddened that his journey in the professional game has come to an end," he said.

"He has played a huge part in a successful period in Hampshire's history over the past five years, reaching four T20 Finals Days, challenging at the top of Division One in the County Championship, and making the final of the One-Day Cup twice."

title: Why Liverpool icon Salah has chosen Trabzonspor
description: Why Mohamed Salah chose Trabzonspor over Saudi Arabia and MLS, and what the move means for him and Turkish football.
fullText:
After months of speculation, Mohamed Salah's next destination has finally been confirmed.

The Liverpool legend agreed a two-year deal, external with Turkish side Trabzonspor on Thursday following the expiry of his contract at Anfield, bringing an end to one of the most successful careers in Premier League history.

For years, Saudi Pro League clubs pursued Salah, while Major League Soccer was also viewed as a realistic destination for one of world football's biggest stars. Instead, the 34-year-old has remained in Europe by joining Trabzonspor, a club better known for upsetting Turkey's established order than dominating it.

So why has Salah chosen Trabzonspor, and what can both player and club expect from one another?

Money alone does not explain Salah's decision. Saudi Arabian clubs had long identified the Egyptian as one of their priority targets, with Al-Ittihad even making a late approach, while Sporting Kansas City were among the MLS clubs interested in bringing him to the United States.

Both destinations could have offered enormous monetary rewards. Instead, Salah opted to stick with European football.

He will be very well paid in Turkey. In a posting to the Turkish stock exchange, Trabzonspor confirmed he will be paid £14.5m per season and will receive a 20% share of revenue from Salah-branded merchandise.

Trabzonspor finished third in last season's Super Lig and will compete in this month's Europa League play-offs. Victory over two legs would see them qualify for the league phase, while defeat would send them into the Conference League.

For a player who helped Egypt reach the knockout stages of this summer's World Cup and produced one of the finest campaigns of his career in 2024-25, continuing to compete in Uefa competition appears to have carried significant weight.

If Salah was determined to stay in Europe, Trabzonspor might not have been the obvious choice.

Turkey's traditional powerhouses are Galatasaray, Fenerbahce and Besiktas, with most of the country's biggest-name arrivals historically choosing one of the Istanbul giants.

Besiktas did attempt to sign Salah before negotiations collapsed over the financial structure of the deal, opening the door for Trabzonspor.

Although they lack the global profile of Turkey's biggest clubs, Trabzonspor are far from outsiders.

They are seven-time Turkish champions, won the Super Lig as recently as 2021-22 and lifted last season's Turkish Cup.

Fatih Tekke's side also finished third in the league, earning another opportunity to qualify for European competition.

Salah instantly becomes the biggest signing in the club's history. The excitement surrounding his arrival underlined that status as hundreds of supporters gathered to welcome him before he travelled on to Trabzon.

Former Scotland midfielder Ryan Jack, who won the Scottish Premiership with Rangers in 2021, has spent the last two seasons playing in Turkey. He was not surprised by the scenes.

"That's one thing about Turkish football - the fans are incredibly passionate," he told BBC Sport. "The big clubs have huge support and they really get behind their teams."

During his unveiling, he briefly wore a symbolic number 61 shirt in tribute to the city, with the number representing Trabzon's vehicle registration code and holding special significance among supporters, who traditionally celebrate the 61st minute of matches.

However, for the 2026-27 season, Salah will wear the number 10 shirt after requesting the number he also wears for Egypt. Team-mate Ernest Muci agreed to relinquish the jersey as a gesture of respect for the club's marquee signing.

Salah's move is the latest sign of Turkish football's growing appeal to established stars.

Victor Osimhen, Leroy Sane, Ilkay Gundogan, Nathan Ake and Leandro Trossard are among the high-profile names now playing in the Super Lig, while Andre Onana, Ruslan Malinovskyi and Stefan Savic are already part of Trabzonspor's squad.

Last summer, the Super Lig recorded the third-highest net transfer spend in world football behind only the Premier League and Saudi Pro League, highlighting the league's increasing ambition.

The economics behind that spending are unusual.

Turkey's biggest clubs generate substantial income in euros through Uefa competition while many domestic operating costs remain in Turkish lira.

The country's prolonged period of high inflation has also reduced the relative value of existing domestic debt, giving clubs greater flexibility than might initially appear.

Financially, Trabzonspor were therefore able to present Salah with an attractive package.

Reports in Turkey say he has signed a two-year contract until June 2028 worth around £7.3m per season, below the salary he could reportedly have earned in Saudi Arabia, with additional bonuses and a share of merchandise revenue linked to his name.

The result is a league capable of offering competitive salaries, passionate fanbases and European football to players entering the latter stages of their careers.

Jack believes the competition's profile is continuing to rise.

"The league is getting stronger every year and you're seeing more and more big names joining," he said.

"Salah is probably the biggest name to move to Turkey in recent years. It shows the league is growing and it might persuade other top players to consider going there. There are great stadiums, great cities and it's a competitive league."

His own experience reinforced that impression.

"I loved it," Jack added. "Everyone helps you settle in and the people are really friendly. When foreign players arrive, the clubs do everything they can to help them."

Despite attracting recognisable names, the Super Lig is some way below Europe's elite competitions.

Opta currently ranks it as the 14th strongest domestic league in world football, behind top-flights in countries such as Denmark, Poland and even England's Championship.

Turkish clubs have also found sustained European success difficult to achieve.

Since Galatasaray won the Uefa Cup in 2000, only one Turkish side has reached the semi-finals of a major Uefa competition, illustrating the gap that still exists between Turkey's biggest clubs and Europe's established powers.

For Salah, however, the move represents a compromise. Rather than stepping away from European football he will continue playing continental competition while competing in one of the most fervent environments.

Age suggests Salah is entering the twilight of his career, but there is evidence he still has plenty to offer.

He inspired Egypt to the knockout stages of the 2026 World Cup, contributing one goal and two assists in five appearances.

His final season at Liverpool proved more difficult as the defending Premier League champions slipped to fifth place amid a disappointing campaign.

Salah scored 12 goals across all competitions after falling out of favour under Arne Slot.

Only a year earlier, he had delivered one of the best individual campaigns of his career, scoring 34 goals and registering 23 assists in all competitions as Liverpool lifted the Premier League title.

Even allowing for his decline last season, few players arriving in Turkey possess anything close to Salah's pedigree.

Trabzonspor are expected to build their attack around him immediately.

Fatih Tekke's side typically operate in a 4-2-3-1, with Salah expected to occupy his familiar position on the right wing, cutting inside onto his stronger left foot in the role that made him one of Europe's most prolific forwards.

Tekke can also switch to a 4-3-3 without majorly altering Salah's responsibilities, leaving the Egyptian as the focal point of the club's attacking threat.

His competitive debut could come on 15 August when Trabzonspor open their Super Lig campaign away to Kasimpasa, before attention quickly turns to a Europa League play-off against either Hungary's Ferencvaros or Poland's Gornik Zabrze.

For Trabzonspor, the transfer extends far beyond what Salah might produce on the pitch.

His arrival immediately raises the club's global profile, boosts commercial opportunities and provides one of the most marketable footballers of the modern era.

Jack also believes Salah's arrival will increase international interest in the Turkish game.

"I think Liverpool fans, and people who love watching Salah, will definitely take notice and start following the league," he said.

"When I moved there, my family and friends started watching games because they didn't really know much about Turkish football before. Salah's move will make people sit up and watch more of the league."

Meanwhile, for Salah, the move offers something perhaps more valuable than another lucrative contract.

He remains in Europe, has the chance to compete for domestic honours and European football, and becomes the undisputed figurehead of one of Turkey's most historic clubs.

It may not have been the destination many expected, but for both player and club, Trabzonspor represents an opportunity to begin an ambitious new chapter.

title: Barcelona? Real Madrid? Man City's Rodri has a decision to make
description: Midfielder Rodri may have a huge decision to make this summer on whether to join Real Madrid or Barcelona, should he decide to leave Manchester City.
fullText:
Manchester City midfielder Rodri may have a huge decision to make this summer on whether to join La Liga giants Real Madrid or Barcelona - should he decide to leave Etihad Stadium.

The 30-year-old is into the final year of his deal at City and is yet to sign fresh terms.

Real have held a long-term interest in signing the player, but two separate sources told BBC Sport on Thursday that Spanish champions Barcelona have joined the race for his signature.

To add to the intrigue, Barca sources have distanced themselves from such talk when approached to comment by BBC Sport.

How do Manchester City manage the Rodri dilemma?

Rodri missed much of the 2024-25 campaign after sustaining a serious knee injury, and parts of last season were disrupted by a hamstring issue.

However, the 2024 Ballon d'Or winner was back to his best at the World Cup in the summer, leading Spain to their second title and being named player of the tournament.

Rodri said earlier this season his future would be sorted out after the tournament, but he is currently out of action after undergoing back surgery.

City are currently on a pre-season tour in the Far East and face Arsenal in the Community Shield next Sunday, but Rodri is yet to link up with his team-mates. Once he does return, he has a major decision to make.

Does he sign the deal that is on offer from City, see out the final months of his contract and become a free agent next summer or take up the tantalising prospect of a return to his homeland?

City sources have previously told BBC Sport they are "counting on" the player for next season, while a significant fee would need to be offered to even consider a sale of the player.

A move to Barca would allow Rodri to join the title winners for the past two seasons and unite with national team compatriots Ferran Torres, Lamine Yamal, Pau Cubarsi and Pedri.

However, he may enjoy a quick reunion with ex-City team-mate Bernardo Silva, who joined Real on a free this summer, and the club will be led by the returning Jose Mourinho.

Rodri, though, may not receive a universal reception if he joins one of the two Spanish giants.

He played for Atletico Madrid in the past and having previously said "you can't turn down the best clubs in the world" with regards to Real, the reception at Nou Camp would be highly interesting if he did end up there.

Rodri has won four Premier League titles, the Champions League and two FA Cups since joining City in 2019 and has established himself as being not only integral to the side, but as one of the best midfielders in the world.

Having already lost Silva this summer, losing Rodri would be a significant blow and would require one of Mateo Kovacic, Nico Gonzalez or Tijjani Reijnders to step up, with all three featuring in pre-season so far.

Club record signing Elliot Anderson is set to be a starter, so there would be a big hole to fill alongside the England international.

City remain in talks to sign 18-year-old midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille, but it would be a big ask for the Moroccan teenager to fill such esteemed boots.

title: Mark Hughes' son died of sudden adult death syndrome
description: Alex Hughes was found collapsed at his home in Macclesfield, Cheshire, on 19 June by his two sons.
fullText:
The son of former Manchester United footballer Mark Hughes died from sudden adult death syndrome, a coroner has found.

Alex Hughes was found collapsed at his home in Macclesfield, Cheshire, on 19 June by his two sons.

The 38-year-old, who followed his ex-Wales international father into football and held roles in recruitment at Grimsby Town, Manchester City and other clubs, could not be revived by paramedics, his inquest heard.

Following his death, Mark Hughes and his wife Jill said they were "totally heartbroken by the sudden and unexpected loss of our beloved son".

Sudden adult death syndrome (SADS) - also known as sudden arrhythmic syndrome - is diagnosed when the cause of death cannot be explained in a post-mortem examination because the structure of the heart appears normal.

It affects about 500 people in the UK every year.

The British Heart Foundation said SADS "usually happens when a dangerously abnormal heart rhythm goes untreated and leads to a cardiac arrest".

The foundation added that inherited heart conditions are "often the cause of SADS if the person who has it doesn't know they do".

In a statement released through the League Managers Association, former Manchester City, Stoke and Blackburn manager Hughes said: "Alex was a wonderful son, brother to Curtis and Xenna, devoted husband and father to Jessica and their two beautiful children Sebastian and Leonardo.

"Alex was player recruitment lead at Grimsby Town FC, and had many good friends and colleagues. He will be so deeply missed by us all."

Alex Hughes had a brief playing career, on the books of Stockport and Wrexham, before joining Blackburn in 2007, working as a performance analyst during his father's time as manager.

He then followed his father to Manchester City in 2008 and worked with him again at Fulham before forging his own path abroad.

The club's head coach David Artell described him as "just such a good guy", adding: "Life can be really cruel."

title: England recall Pope & Lawrence for Pakistan Tests but Bethell out
description: Surrey duo Ollie Pope and Dan Lawrence are recalled to the England squad for the first two Tests against Pakistan.
fullText:
Surrey duo Ollie Pope and Dan Lawrence have been recalled to the England squad for the first two Tests against Pakistan.

The pair have been named in a 16-man squad before the series opener at Headingley on Wednesday 19 August but Jacob Bethell will miss the entire series through injury, with Jordan Cox to be promoted to number three.

The three-match series marks England's first Test outing since the retirement of captain Ben Stokes and sacking of head coach Brendon McCullum.

Joe Root will captain the side for the first time since being reappointed to the role in July, with Marcus Trescothick serving as interim head coach. McCullum's replacement, Stephen Fleming, will begin his tenure against South Africa in December.

England's 16-man squad for the first two Tests against Pakistan: Joe Root (c), Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson, Shoaib Bashir, Harry Brook, Brydon Carse, Sam Cook, Jordan Cox, Ben Duckett, Matthew Fisher, Emilio Gay, Dan Lawrence, Ollie Pope, Ollie Robinson, Jamie Smith, Josh Tongue.

Lawrence, who earned the last of his 14 Test caps in September 2024, is rewarded for his domestic form. The 29-year-old is the second-highest run-scorer in Division One of the County Championship, with 788 runs at 65.66, including five centuries, in 13 innings.

He is slated to bat at six, filling a middle-order vacancy created by Stokes' retirement, but is far from a like-for-like replacement for the former captain.

Only Gus Atkinson (79 wickets) has taken more Test wickets for England than Stokes (78) since the start of June 2022. Lawrence, who bowls right-arm off-spin, has taken nine wickets from 178.2 overs in the County Championship this season.

There is no place in the squad for Sam Curran or Rehan Ahmed, who had both been tipped to replace Stokes.

"We have selected a squad for the first two Tests that balances rising talent with the experience needed against a quality Pakistan team," said England's men's national selector, Marcus North.

"Sam Curran is a player of real value and interest in terms of that role. He's had a heavy summer workload and he's been playing at the highest level with a number of niggles and we don't feel he's quite right at the moment for this Test squad.

"Rehan has done nothing wrong - he's someone we highly regard. At this stage we felt that going in with what we see as our best six batters with Smudge [Jamie Smith] at seven is key. That's why Lawrence has got the nod at six."

Former vice-captain Pope was replaced by Bethell at number three for the final two Ashes Tests in Australia following an extended period of poor form and was subsequently dropped from the squad against New Zealand.

Like Lawrence, he has performed well in the County Championship, scoring 510 runs at 56.66, including five 50+ knocks, for Surrey, but will not automatically slot back into the side in Bethell's absence.

Bethell suffered a knee injury during the ODI series against India in July and is set to be replaced by Cox, who made his Test debut against New Zealand at The Oval.

Essex's Sam Cook returns to the squad for the first time since last summer. The 29-year-old seamer made his international debut against Zimbabwe in May 2025 and was named in the squad for the five-match series against India but did not feature.

Brydon Carse returns after a broken wrist ruled him out of the Indian Premier League and the start of the Test summer while England are sticking with spinner Shoaib Bashir, who featured in the first and third Tests against New Zealand after being overlooked during the Ashes.

North also confirmed new head coach Fleming was involved in selecting the squad despite not taking over the role formally until after the Pakistan series.

"Stephen Fleming was involved in a lot of discussions," said North. "I think that was really important.

"Certainly from my perspective, as soon as he got appointed, I reached out and we had long conversations. It was important that our selection reflects the strategy and thinking long term moving into the winter when Stephen takes over the team."

North was also asked about the prospect of former captain Stokes reversing his international retirement.

"Ben made the decision to retire and it's great to see him playing well and enjoying his cricket at Durham," he said.

"But until he reverses that decision and does become available for selection my job is to look at the players that are, and make sure that we become a strong, competitive England cricket team and work our way up those Test world rankings."

Analysis by BBC cricket reporter Henry Moeran

For those who were hoping for a brave new world, there may be disappointment. This is a squad with plenty of familiar faces and no potential debutants.

Ollie Pope and Brydon Carse return for the first time since the Ashes and Dan Lawrence is selected two years on from his last Test appearance

The big question was who was going to replace Ben Stokes as the all-rounder but that isn't entirely obvious.

There is no place for Sam Curran, James Coles or Rehan Ahmed, who is dropped, which means Lawrence might find his part-time spin plays a significant role.

North was keen to emphasise the strength in depth in English cricket, despite the lack of fresh names in the squad. Curran is someone we can expect to see sooner rather than later as the all-rounder gap looks to be filled.

As for Ollie Pope - dropped after a miserable Ashes - his selection is one of a supporting leadership role and back-up as opposed to likely selection: should England lose a senior batter to injury it would leave them painfully short of experience.

Many have suggested Sam Cook doesn't have the pace to perform at Test level but his red-ball skill remains unquestionable - 27 wickets for Essex this year in just six matches is some record.
