title: La Liga club stand firm on €16 million price tag for Barcelona defensive target
description: Barcelona have not made any defensive reinforcements this summer but have different players on their radar.The Catalan club have been tracking the progress of Racing Santander player Jorge Salinas, bu...
fullText:
Barcelona have not made any defensive reinforcements this summer but have different players on their radar.

The Catalan club have been tracking the progress of Racing Santander player Jorge Salinas, but a move has not transpired so far.

Barça wanted to complete the move before 1 July, insisting that his release clause was €8 million, since Racing had not officially been promoted to La Liga.

However, the newly-promoted club have insisted on the €16 million release clause from the outset, leaving the two clubs apart in negotiations.

Speaking about Salinas' future, as quoted by Mundo Deportivo, Racing sporting director Chema Aragon insisted the versatile defender will only leave if a club triggers his €16 million release clause.

Barcelona remain keen on Salinas. (Photo by Juan Manuel Serrano Arce/Getty Images)

Barcelona's current valuation is significantly lower, with the Catalan club prepared to offer around €6 million.

Aragon admitted that Racing would struggle to stop one of Europe's biggest clubs if the clause is paid, but stressed that the club's priority is to keep hold of one of their brightest young talents.

"We want our best players to stay," he said, while acknowledging that "there is little you can do if a giant comes along and pays the clause."

Despite the growing transfer speculation, Aragon revealed that Salinas has handled the situation impeccably.

The Racing director described the teenager's attitude as "exemplary", praising the defender for returning to pre-season in excellent condition and never attempting to force a move away from the club.

He also confirmed that Racing are prepared to reward the youngster with an improved contract if he remains beyond the end of the transfer window.

Jorge Salinas' release clause stands at €16 million. (Photo courtesy: Instagram/@jorgesaliiinas)

"If he stays, we'll have to recognize his growth in his contract as well," Aragon explained.

Salinas' ability to operate both as a left-back and a central defender makes him an attractive option for Barcelona, particularly given the club's focus on signing young players with positional versatility.

However, the sizeable gap between Racing's €16 million valuation and Barcelona's reported €6 million offer means there is currently no obvious path to an agreement.

If Barça are that keen to sign the Under-19 Euros champion, they will have to increase their offer significantly for the newly promoted club to consider it.

Salinas is not a priority for Barcelona this summer, but he is a developmental bet who can explode in the future.

It is up to Deco now to figure out how to sweeten the deal and convince Racing to sell Salinas in the coming weeks.

description: On the latest Albion Unlimited podcast, BBC Radio Sussex's Johnny Cantor is joined by former Brighton forward Warren Aspinall as they discuss the Seagulls' possible opponents in the Conference League play-off tie.  Brighton will face CFR Cluj (Romania) or Tromso (Norway) in the key fixture. fullText:
On the latest Albion Unlimited podcast, BBC Radio Sussex's Johnny Cantor is joined by former Brighton forward Warren Aspinall as they discuss the Seagulls' possible opponents in the Conference League play-off tie.

Brighton will face CFR Cluj (Romania) or Tromso (Norway) in the key fixture.

Cluj and Tromso are yet to face each other in their two-legged tie, but Cantor believes Tromso could pose a "potential banana skin" for Fabian Hurzeler's side.

"They are placed third in the Norwegian season, which is deep into the campaign as they play across the summer," said Cantor.

In Tromso's Norwegian Eliteserien campaign, they have lost two out of 16 possible games.

In the Romanian SuperLiga, Cluj are also in fourth position, but they have only played three games in the 2026-27 campaign.

Cluj and Tromso's second leg tie will be played on 13 August, with the winner facing Brighton in a two-legged tie on 20 and 27 August, with the Seagulls at home for the second leg.

title: Vote now to crown the Gardner-area high school sports Team of the Year
description: Nine local high school teams are vying for Team of the Year. See the nominees and cast your vote today.
fullText:
The summer is offseason for high school sports, making it the perfect time to reflect on the big year area teams and athletes had over the fall, winter and spring seasons.

The Gardner News has already looked at the Moment of the Year and Coach of the Year, and now it's time to check out which team reigns supreme.

These are the top teams up for Team of the Year. They were chosen as nominees for their success, taking into consideration factors such as final record, participation in the state tournament and team or individual accomplishments.

Check out the top nine teams that made the poll. Vote for which you think was the best of Gardner-area sports for 2025-26. The poll will run until noon on August 17.

The Warriors had a successful season this fall. They finished 7-4 and were second in Mid-Wach D standings. They earned the No. 15 seed in the Div. 8 state tournament and fell in the quarterfinals to Lee. Senior defensive end Brandon Rene was a major competitor, earning 73 tackles 5.5 sacks in the position, which was new to him this season. He earned Mid-Wach All Star honors, was named the Div. 8 All-Star Team Defensive MVP and also won The Gardner News Football Player of the Year.

Quabbin field hockey earned a 16-4-1 record, were Mid-Wach B League Champions and earned the No. 7 seed in the Div. 4 state tournament. They made a run to the Elite Eight before being knocked out by eventual state champion, Dennis-Yarmouth. Maria Hamm, Makenzie Casey and Abby Rogowski led the team from all aspects on the field.

The Wildcats have been consistent over the past several years on the soccer field. This fall, they were 15-3-1, second in Mid-Wach D and advanced to the Elite Eight in the state tournament. Senior Cam Gamache led the league in scoring with 20 goals and 14 assists. Sophomore Gabe Carvalho contributed 17 goals and 7 assists.

More: Gardner High football looks to bounce back in 2026: See the schedule

Monty Tech had a strong year, finishing 12-6 and third in the newly formed CMAC E league. They earned seven shutouts, had a 3.6 goals scored average and qualified for the Div. 3 state tournament. Freshman Addison Boudreau led the team in scoring with 23 goals and 11 assists to land second in league scoring standings and seventh in all of Central Mass.

The Warriors had a breakout season this winter after earning their first winning season since 2020. With a final record of 18-4, they qualified for both the Clark Tournament and the state tournament. Senior Max Kauffman cemented his name in the record books by becoming a 1,000-point scorer.

Oakmont girls basketball had a major goal on their list going into the winter: win the Clark Tournament- and they did just that. They earned the one seed and became the large school bracket champions. They finished their season 15-7 and earned a spot in the state tournament as well. Olivia Martin, Lucie Horgan, Jada LeBlanc and Allie McLaughlin led the team as captains.

More: See what readers voted as The Gardner News Moment of the Year

Gardner has improved each season since the varsity baseball program was reinstated three years ago. They were 11-7, qualified for the postseason and won their first playoff game in 13 years. Andrew Beauregard led on the mound with a 7-2 record and 2.57 ERA. Cam Gamache has a .634 batting average, 33 hits, 24 RBIs and broke the school record for bases stolen with 46.

The Warriors were 15-6 this spring, landing at second in Mid-Wach D standings and earned the No. 19 seed in the Div. 4 state tournament. Gianna Manca led with a .586 batting average, 36 runs and 28 RBIs.

Oakmont had another successful spring on their quest for their ultimate goal of a state championship. Though they fell short of that, they still had plenty of strong moments. They were 16-4 and second in Mid-Wach B and earned the No. 10 seed in the Div. 3 tournament. Quin Buckley and Brayden Nally both surpassed 200 career points, Jack Norris accomplished 800 career faceoff wins and Silas Roy was named a USA Lacrosse All-American.

title: Antonelli opens up about outstanding season so far: 'I didn't expect this'
description: Kimi Antonelli leads the drivers' standings heading into the Formula 1 summer break. The Italian has been satisfied with his season so far, but stressed that the job is far from finished.
fullText:
Kimi Antonelli leads the drivers' standings heading into the Formula 1 summer break. The Italian has been satisfied with his season so far, but stressed that the job is far from finished.

The young Italian has impressed so far in the 2026 Formula 1 season. After finishing second behind George Russell in Australia, he won five Grands Prix in a row.

Car issues hampered Antonelli at the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya and Silverstone, but he bounced back by winning at Spa-Francorchamps before securing another podium finish at the Hungaroring.

As a result, he holds a 50-point lead over Lewis Hamilton and a 59-point advantage over Russell at the halfway point of the season.

Looking back at the season so far, Antonelli said: "Well, for sure, I did not expect to find myself in this position. But, you know, the car has been extremely good, the team has done an incredible job and, on my side, I try to maximize every opportunity I have."

The Mercedes driver added: "Of course, there's still lots of work to do, lots to learn, but it was a good first half of the season. Now I'm looking forward to the second half and we're just going to keep pushing."

Despite his lead in the standings, former Formula 1 driver Gerhard Berger is not ready to back Antonelli over Russell in the title fight, pointing to last season as proof that the championship can quickly swing after Oscar Piastri appeared to be the clear favorite midway through the year.

He said to F1.com: "I don't think it's the right way to put money on it (who becomes world champion). One is the risky, young, hot blood, the other is already much more experienced and will play the ball back into Antonelli's field. Last year, in the beginning, it looked like Oscar Piastri was going to beat Lando Norris, and Norris turned the page around and won the championship. That's all open in F1. It will be open until the end."

title: How could Newcastle play under Jaissle?
description: Matthias Jaissle's predecessor Eddie Howe had similar principles in terms of building a side around physical intensity, pressing and direct attacks.  Howe's defensive tactics should align well with the Red Bull Salzburg style of pressing, which could make it easier for the players to buy into Jaissle's methods.  What Howe was criticised for towards the end of his tenure, though, was a supposed lack of adaptability.
fullText:
Matthias Jaissle's predecessor Eddie Howe had similar principles in terms of building a side around physical intensity, pressing and direct attacks.

The German primarily uses a high-pressing 4-4-2 when the opposition are building from the back.

Even when his teams are pushed into more of a mid-block, they have shown an impressive understanding of when to step forward and transition into a high press as a collective.

Howe's defensive tactics should align well with the Red Bull Salzburg style of pressing, which could make it easier for the players to buy into Jaissle's methods.

What Howe was criticised for towards the end of his tenure, though, was a supposed lack of adaptability.

After joining Al-Ahli, Jaissle inherited a mosaic of superstars and less experienced Saudi players - a wildly different challenge from coaching a Red Bull club with consistency and understanding in style from youth level through to first team.

While he retained his coaching principles, he recognised the need to platform players according to their individual strengths within that framework.

The Premier League is constantly evolving, with coaches designing new counter-measures to tactics that appear to work from one week to the next.

If Jaissle is going to succeed in the English top flight, that agility will be a vital asset.

title: Check out the Johannesburg-Lewiston high school football schedule
description: Johannesburg-Lewiston football hopes to find success in a new-look Northern Michigan Football Conference; take a look at their 2026 schedule breakdown.
fullText:
JOHANNESBURG ― We're on team three of three of our Gaylord area high school football schedule breakdowns. Next week, teams will be back on the field for the first official practices of the 2026 season. We've covered what Gaylord and Gaylord St. Mary are looking forward to this year ― now it's Johannesburg-Lewiston's turn.

It would've been hard to predict the past five years of JoBurg football when they left the Thirbly Field in Traverse City on Jan. 16, 2021 after the Division 8 state semifinals. One of Northern Michigan's most consistent programs in the 2010s is now 5-38 in the last five seasons. With a new-look conference yet a familiar-looking schedule, will this be the year JoBurg returns to its winning ways?

St. Mary GSM football enters new conference, faces new look schedule in 2026

GHS Gaylord High School football schedule breakdown, 2026

Last matchup: Tawas 21, JoBurg 6 (Sept. 13, 2024)

A few more teams left the Northern Michigan Football Conference this offseason, prompting the league to officially ditch the divisions and reformat as a nine-team conference with an eight-game schedule. That makes this game, formerly a cross-divisional battle, a season opener and league opener for both teams.

Tawas and JL both finished 1-8 last year, making this a key battle for both teams to gauge their progress.

It's somewhat hard to believe these two programs have never crossed paths on the football field, but it will now be an annual event in the NMFC as JL heads to Bezonia in Week 2. Benzie Central went 2-7 in 2026 but had solid offensive showings against Tawas (56-0) and Oscoda (54-12).

Sept. 11 vs. Oscoda (Military Appreciation Night)

Last matchup: JoBurg 26, Oscoda 14 (Oct. 3, 2025)

JL got its lone win of the 2025 season at Oscoda in Week 6 last year. Now, they host the Owls in Week 3, a chance for the Cardinals to pick up a league victory in the new-look NMFC.

Last matchup: Frankfort 41, JoBurg 30 (Sept. 12, 2025)

The game against Frankfort may have been JL's best showing in 2025, losing by just 11 points to a future playoff team. Where JL stands after Week 4 will say a lot about this team's progression, so use this as a measuring stick matchup in about a month.

Sept. 25 at Maple City Glen Lake

Last matchup: Glen Lake 49, JoBurg 6 (Oct. 10, 2025)

Maple City Glen Lake won the final NMFC-Legacy Championship and a Division 8 district championship in 2025. Now, they enter the new NMFC as a top contender to win another league title.

Last matchup: Mancelona 44, JoBurg 6 (Oct. 17, 2025)

The wheels had fallen off for JL by the time the Ironmen came to town, but Mancy showed just how big the gap was between the Cardinals and the top half of the league when they rolled through JoBurg late last season.

Last matchup: EJ 51, JoBurg 0 (Sept. 5, 2025)

This Week 2 shutout was a disappointment for JL's coaches after a solid performance against Burton Bendle in Week 1. Now, JL will have more than a few weeks to prepare for a team that owns a five-game win streak over the Cardinals, but will need to bring a healthy team to EJ for a chance at an upset victory.

Last matchup: Harbor 45, JoBurg 12 (Sept. 19, 2025)

Despite the struggles of the last five years, JL could usually count on at least one league win when they played Harbor Springs. That changed in 2025, leaving the Cardinals without a league win for the first time since 2021.

The league finale for JL, this is a major final test for how far the JLHS program has progressed.

Last matchup: Manton 50, JoBurg 8 (Oct. 24, 2025)

JL and Manton have met in Week 9 each of the last five seasons: different matchup, same story for JL. The Rangers have won five straight over the Cardinals, last year's 42-point victory being the most lopsided of the five matchups. JoBurg's lone non-conference gam, this matchup featured a playoff team last year; JoBurg hopes it will feature two this season.

title: Salisbury University announces Justin Axel as new Head Men's Lacrosse Coach
description: Salisbury University has named Justin Axel as the new head coach of their men's lacrosse team.
fullText:
Justin Axel has been hired as Salisbury University's new head men's lacrosse coach, the school announced on Tuesday.

Axel, a Salisbury alum who has served as an assistant coach for the Sea Gulls during two different stints, will be taking over as head coach after longtime head coach Jim Berkman announced his retirement in June.

"This is a special moment for Salisbury men's lacrosse, and Justin is the right person to lead the program forward," Salisbury University Director of Athletics and Campus Recreation Monica Polizzi said in a statement. "He understands what makes Sea Gull lacrosse different because he has helped build its championship tradition for more than a decade. Justin brings championship experience, proven leadership and a deep commitment to developing student-athletes on and off the field. We are confident he will continue the standard of excellence that has made SU one of the premier programs in collegiate lacrosse."

Under Berkman's leadership, Salisbury's men's lacrosse team became one of the premier programs in Division III, winning 13 national titles. Now, Axel will look to continue that success as the new head coach.

"It is a true honor to build upon the incredible legacy of Coach Jim Berkman and Salisbury Men's Lacrosse," Axel said about his hiring. "I am extremely excited about the future of this program and the opportunities that lie ahead. I want to thank President Lepre and Athletic Director Monica Polizzi for this incredible opportunity. Coach Berkman has been an instrumental figure in my life, and I cannot thank him enough for his support, guidance, and friendship over the last 25 years. I am also deeply grateful for the unwavering support of my wife, Meaghan, and my daughter, Sloan—coaching is a family endeavor, and their love and understanding mean everything. I am truly honored to lead this program forward."

Axel first served as an assistant coach for Salisbury from 2002 to 2007, during which the Sea Gulls won four national championships. Axel went on to become the head coach at Eastern Connecticut State in 2007, where his teams recorded an 81-42 record and won four Little East Conference titles during his tenure.

Axel returned to Salisbury in 2014, becoming the recruiting director and assistant coach for the Sea Gulls. Salisbury has won three more national titles since 2014. During their most recent national championship season in 2023, Axel was named the Intercollegiate Men's Lacrosse Coaches Association Division III Assistant Coach of the Year.

Advanced Python Scheduler (APScheduler) is a task scheduler and task queue system for
Python. It can be used solely as a job queuing system if you have no need for task
scheduling. It scales both up and down, and is suitable for both trivial, single-process
use cases as well as large deployments spanning multiple nodes. Multiple schedulers and
workers can be deployed to use a shared data store to provide both a degree of high
availability and horizontal scaling.

APScheduler comes in both synchronous and asynchronous flavors, making it a good fit for
both traditional, thread-based applications, and asynchronous (asyncio or Trio)
applications. Documentation and examples are provided for integrating with either WSGI
or ASGI compatible web applications.

Support is provided for persistent storage of schedules and jobs. This means that they
can be shared among multiple scheduler/worker instances and will survive process and
node restarts.

title: Nix Overrides That Expire Themselves
description: Package overrides in a Nix flake tend to outlive the problem they were written to solve. A small trick with lib.warnIf makes an override announce when nixpkgs has caught up and the override can be deleted.
fullText:
July 30th, 2026

 | Warsaw, Poland

I recently published yesod-form-1.7.10 to Hackage. My project gets all of its
dependencies from nixpkgs, and nixpkgs gradually adopts Haskell packages from
Hackage. That means that there’s some time between when the package lands in
nixpkgs, and when I need to use the package in my project, which is right now.

You can write an override in your flake.nix to get the newer package you
need, but what happens when you eventually bump the nixpkgs version and the
override is made redundant? There’s nothing by default which warns you that the
override should be removed.

A colleague of mine showed me this pattern which makes the override announce
its own obsolescence. When Nix evaluates the flake, it compares package
versions and warns when the version is greater than or equal to the version in
your override.

In this example, hprev.yesod-form.version is whatever the pinned nixpkgs
provides. The lib.versionAtLeast function compares version strings, and
lib.warnIf is the part that prints a message during evaluation when the
condition is true.

So, when it’s time to remove the override, you’ll see something like this:

This approach isn’t specific to package versions. You can do this anywhere you
have an override where the justification for the override can be expressed
conditionally. For example, we also use this to clean up overrides where a
package was marked as broken in nixpkgs, and is subsequently un-marked.

When someone eventually fixes the package upstream and the broken flag is
removed, the warning tells us to delete the workaround.

title: China's first sodium-ion electric dump truck enters service
description: Chinese companies Hina Battery and Tonly Heavy Industries say they have delivered the world's first all-electric dump truck powered by a sodium-ion battery.
fullText:
Chinese companies Hina Battery and Tonly Heavy Industries say they have delivered the world's first all-electric dump truck powered by a sodium-ion battery. The project highlights the growing adoption of this cell chemistry in commercial vehicles, even though its energy density still trails that of lithium-ion batteries.

The range of applications for sodium-ion batteries is expanding in China. Following their use in stationary energy storage systems, passenger cars and heavy-duty trucks, Hina Battery and Tonly Heavy Industries have now delivered what they describe as the world’s first battery-electric dump truck powered by a sodium-ion battery. The vehicle was handed over to mining company Sanyou Mining in July and will generate real-world operational data to support the further development of the technology.

The vehicle is based on Tonly’s TLE120 platform and is equipped with Hina Battery’s ‘Haixing’ sodium-ion battery system, which offers a storage capacity of 676 kWh. According to the manufacturer, the cells achieve an energy density of more than 165 Wh/kg. The battery can be fully charged in 20 to 25 minutes and is designed to deliver more than 8,000 charge cycles, even under regular fast-charging conditions.

The developers highlight the advantages of sodium-ion cell chemistry for mining applications in particular. Sodium-ion batteries are considered well suited to low-temperature operation and offer high cycle stability – both key requirements in mining, where vehicles often run in multi-shift operations and face extreme winter conditions. Hina Battery also says the technology enables smaller battery packs, shorter charging times and higher vehicle availability.

The latest deployment forms part of a broader trend in China. In June, FAW Jiefang announced the completion of extensive road tests of a heavy-duty electric truck equipped with a sodium-ion battery from Hina Battery. The vehicle covered more than 15,000 kilometres over almost seven months. According to FAW, the battery retained more than 90% of its usable capacity at temperatures as low as -40 degrees Celsius and is designed to achieve more than 8,000 fast-charging cycles.

Several Chinese battery manufacturers are advancing the commercialisation of sodium-ion technology in parallel. In May, CATL announced an investment of five billion yuan to expand its sodium-ion battery production capacity to 40 GWh per year. A month later, the company said it plans to equip up to 20,000 vehicles with the new battery technology this year. BYD has reported up to 10,000 charge cycles for its developmental cells, while BAIC has already presented prototypes with an energy density of over 170 Wh/kg.

However, sodium-ion technology still faces economic challenges compared to lithium-ion batteries. According to Hina Battery, sodium-ion cells currently cost between 0.5 and 0.7 yuan per Wh, compared with 0.3 to 0.5 yuan per Wh for lithium-ion cells. CEO Li Shujun expects the costs of both chemistries to converge by 2027 or 2028, with cell costs falling to around 0.3 yuan per Wh by 2028.

The technology also continues to lag behind lithium-ion batteries in terms of energy density. Last year, Tonly introduced a battery-electric dump truck with an 801 kWh LFP battery, compared with the 676 kWh sodium-ion battery used in the newly unveiled model. In addition, Tonly has already been offering a battery-swapping system for mining trucks for some time.

title: Nobody Wants to Burn Out Anymore
description: Nobody Wants to Burn Out Anymore
fullText:
You've probably heard it countless times: "Nobody wants to work anymore." It shows up everywhere, from casual conversations to headlines and social media posts.

But here is the catch: this is not a new complaint. It is (way, wayyy) older than you think.

Before we get into it, a quick note about me: I am writing this as a student. I can work less than full time because my parents support me. That is a privilege, not a moral flex. I am not trying to speak for every young person. I am pushing back on a narrative that keeps getting recycled while the deal around work keeps shifting.

Also, I am going to mix countries and examples in this post. Some links are Austrian, some are German and some are US focused. The underlying pattern still matters, but the exact numbers and institutions differ by country.

Take a look at the graphic below, or read Snopes' detailed fact check with sources on the origin of the phrase "nobody wants to work anymore". It shows that this exact phrase has been circulating since at least 1894. For over 130 years, people have accused younger generations of being lazy, entitled or unwilling to put in the effort.

And yet, generation after generation, people keep working.

So no, it is not really about work ethic. When someone says "nobody wants to work anymore", what they usually mean is "nobody wants to work the way I had to."

There is pride in hardship and there is also resentment that can show up when younger generations push back against norms that used to be non-negotiable. Add to that a reluctance to acknowledge that the economic and social reality has changed. Housing prices are astronomically higher in Austria according to Statistik Austria. Job security is increasingly fragile in many sectors, as discussed in a research review on job security and insecurity. Wages and bargaining power have also been a pressure point for a long time, with discussion about long term labor movement effects in this working paper by Cullen.

It is easier to frame all of this as laziness than to admit that the system people are inheriting is often tense, expensive and disrespectful. Surveys of people who actually quit jobs tend to point to low pay, no advancement and feeling disrespected, as summarized in Pew Research Center's survey on why workers quit in 2021.

If you work in hospitality, retail or any kind of service job, the frustration is real. Places are understaffed. Waiting times are longer. People quit and do not come back.

Sometimes you also meet people who are unreliable, checked out or genuinely done. That happens.

A lot of this debate is also about visibility. Plenty of young adults spend longer in education. Many work part time while studying, then disappear during exams, internships or thesis phases. If you are the person trying to staff a shift, that can look like "nobody shows up."

Demographics matter too. If a society gets older, you can get shortages even if nobody changes their attitude. So yes, the surface level impression has some basis. The question is what explains it best.

COVID did not create these tensions, but it cracked them open. What many commentators called "the Great Resignation" often looked less like a tantrum and more like a reassessment, which is how the Financial Times described the phenomenon.

People had time to ask themselves whether they really wanted to return to jobs that left them drained, underpaid and barely able to keep up with their bills. A Pew Research Center survey of workers who quit in 2021 lists boring reasons: low pay, no opportunities for advancement and feeling disrespected.

Then you add inflation. Brookings discusses whether pay has kept up with inflation. If a job does not buy stability, and it also demands your health and your weekends, it is not a mystery why people avoid it.

It is not that people do not want to work. It is that people do not want to sacrifice their health, dignity and future just to stay afloat.

It is a tempting story because it makes the world simple. It also ignores what is actually happening.

For example, some recent reporting suggests that employment among younger age groups has risen in recent years, driven in part by students working alongside education. National Geographic Germany discusses how much Gen Z works compared to previous years and points to German labor market data.

That does not mean every young person is grinding 60 hours a week. It means the "they just do not want to work" storyline is a lazy shortcut.

Also, a lot of young workers are not rejecting work. They are rejecting bullshit jobs. By that I mean: low pay, high stress, no upside and zero respect.

Mental health is another factor that is easy to mock and hard to ignore. People still want to work, they just want more control over their time, which is the core argument in Harvard Business Review's piece on control over time. Gen Z and Millennials also talk more openly about mental well being, and they are more willing to take time off when something is wrong, as described in Verywell Health's report on Gen Z sick days.

This is not only a vibes argument. The American Psychological Association reports that Gen Z adults show high levels of stress and mental health symptoms compared to other age groups in their reporting.

If a job leaves people sick, numb or hopeless, maybe the question should not be "why do they not want to work?" Maybe it should be "why is this still considered acceptable?"

When people say they want "better work", they usually mean boring basics: decent pay, predictable schedules, fair treatment and tasks that do not feel soul crushing.

That is not entitlement. That is a workforce reacting to incentives.

Worker surveys often mention flexibility as one of several reasons people leave or refuse certain jobs, including in Pew Research Center's survey on job quitting reasons. In German speaking debates, you see similar themes around flexible work and fair pay in Der Standard's article on Gen Z work expectations. You also see workplace orgs talk about what makes younger employees actually motivated in Great Place To Work Austria's blog post on Gen Z effort and unions frame it as a necessary adaptation for employers in ÖGB's commentary on employers needing to adapt.

Also, be careful with generational stereotypes in general. A useful discussion of that is the WSI Institute piece Jung, faul, wehleidig? Hat die Gen Z den Generationenvertrag gekündigt?. The point is not that one age group is great and another is bad. The point is that commitment, motivation and expectations depend heavily on conditions, life phase and culture.

Not every job can be remote. Not every workplace can offer full flexibility. Some work is physically hard by nature. That makes the question sharper, not softer: why are the jobs that must be on site so often the ones with the worst pay and the least respect?

People do want to work. They just do not want to be treated like disposable parts in a machine.

So maybe the issue is not that nobody wants to work anymore. Maybe it's that nobody wants to work like it's still 1980 with worse rent and better coffee.

It is also worth saying out loud that a lot of the tension is about fairness. Many older workers suffered through inflexible jobs, toxic bosses and zero room to complain. In Austria, reforms associated with people like Bruno Kreisky shifted parts of that landscape.

So when a younger person says "no thanks" to the same misery, it can sting. It can feel like someone is skipping the struggle you had to endure.

But is that not the point of progress?

If the next generation can demand better working conditions, that is not a moral decline. It is a signal that the old deal stopped making sense. It is also a chance to rebuild it, instead of turning exhaustion into a tradition.

And yes, sometimes the criticism hits home for people like me, too. I get support. I get options. That is exactly why I am not buying the "everyone is just lazy" line. The problem is not young people. The problem is that too many jobs are structured in a way that only works if someone else silently subsidizes your survival, whether that is parents, a partner or your future pension.

Speaking of pensions: plenty of young people do not feel confident they will get one, and that anxiety is part of how they judge the tradeoffs of work and life, as discussed in VersicherungsFinanz's piece on what young people expect and fear about pensions. Public discussions around early retirement in Germany also show how widespread the desire to exit earlier can be and how quickly debates turn into moral judgments, as covered by MDR on early retirement and policy debates.

If the promised finish line looks fuzzy, it is not shocking that people start questioning the race.

title: A Security Pro Hacked North Korean Hackers. He Found They'd Breached Hundreds
description: For nearly two years, researcher Vangelis Stykas has maintained access to North Korean hackers’ servers. His work shows they pulled off intrusions in a shocking number of systems across the globe.
fullText:
North Korea’s stealthy hackers and scam IT workers have infiltrated companies, stealing corporate secrets and plundering billions in cryptocurrency to help fund the totalitarian regime and its weapons programs. Now, a security researcher who has spent almost two years inside the systems belonging to a group of those North Korean hackers is raising the alarm on just how effective and far reaching the targeting of individual employees and contractors has been in breaching organizations across the globe.

Since Greece-based cybersecurity researcher Vangelis Stykas gained access to North Korean systems 22 months ago, he says, he has found evidence that 1,640 companies across 57 countries have been impacted by the country’s hacking operations. Among these, Stykas will detail at the Black Hat security conference in Las Vegas today, around 700 to 800 of the impacted organizations have had “really damaging” intrusions.

“It’s company access, it’s root access to servers, it’s root access to AWS,” the researcher tells WIRED, referring to Amazon Web Services and the term “root” to mean the highest level of permissions in a computer system. “For crypto companies, it’s keys, it’s blockchain access—it’s ridiculous access.”

Stykas, the CTO at cybersecurity firm Kumio, says he accessed multiple command-and-control servers used by the hackers, though he asked WIRED not to reveal the details of how he gained that access due to the sensitivity of that information. In some cases, he notes, the hackers appeared to have infected themselves with their own malware—which, as a result, gave him access to the hackers’ workstations, too. “I have access to their Slack, I have access to their Discord, I have access to a lot of stuff,” Stykas says, adding he has seen around 5 terabytes of data in total.

As he probed those systems over months, Stykas identified potential victims—by analyzing developer keys, source code, and more—and says he has disclosed the incidents to those impacted. As part of his talk at Black Hat, Stykas is publicly naming around a dozen of the impacted companies—these are, he says, largely the ones that handled the disclosures well and/or fixed possible compromises. The researcher says these include the Boston Children’s Hospital (which held a vast Covid-19 database of Americans’ personal health data), the large Japanese tech firm AEON Smart Technology, Chinese phone manufacturer Oppo, cryptocurrency firms Coinbase and Uniswap Labs, Italy’s Supreme Judicial Council, a subsidiary of Saudi Arabian bank Al Rajhi Bank, and Digitaal Vlaanderen, part of the Flemish Government in Belgium.

Multiple companies and organizations named in this article did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment about the incidents. Japan’s Computer Emergency Response Team says it confirmed the security researcher’s findings and worked with AEON Smart Technology on “remediation.”

“We can confirm that we were notified of this incident on March 3, 2026 by the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB), following the researcher’s disclosure,” a spokesperson for the Flemish government says. “As part of that response, the affected workstation was isolated and the potentially exposed credentials and access were revoked and rotated. Based on our investigation, the incident has been contained and remediated.”

A spokesperson for Boston Children’s Hospital says that the incident “involved a former independent contractor's personal device” and not the hospital’s systems. “Upon notification, our cybersecurity and IT teams immediately investigated, disabled any remaining active access credentials within hours, and found no evidence of unauthorized access to Boston Children's systems,” the spokesperson says, adding that the “data at issue” was already publicly available.

Meanwhile, a Coinbase spokesperson says they investigated a contractor, who they found was in the United States, and “uncovered no evidence that he was either located in North Korea nor affiliated with the DPRK government” before it was reported by the researcher, using DPRK to refer to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. “However, our security controls identified potential risks in their technology setup, suggesting they may have outsourced their work to a third party, and we terminated the contractor within 30 days of onboarding, prior to receiving a tip from Vangelis Stykas,” the spokesperson says. They add that “no sensitive information was compromised and no customer data was exposed.”

title: Jeff Dean: The 1% Rule for Building in AI
description: Startup School 2026:

title: Nobody Asked for AI
description: We tend to think that markets reflect consumer choice. But the artificial-intelligence boom has been powered by the investment decisions of concentrated capital rather than by consumer demand.
fullText:
The Big Tech companies have spent $1 trillion on capital investment since the start of the artificial-intelligence boom. Pretty much all that investment has been used to build data centers, purchase the chips that power those data centers, and construct the energy systems that fuel and cool them.

That $1 trillion could have been used for anything. It could have been invested in renewables. It could have been used to develop lifesaving new drugs. It could have been used to build housing, public infrastructure, or anything else human beings need to survive and thrive.

Instead, it has been channeled into constructing energy-draining, water-absorbing data centers that power large language models (LLMs) built on the theft of millions of people’s creative work, which consistently produce incorrect responses and drive many users mad in the process. It’s hard to think of a worse use of society’s shared resources.

Now, you may argue that we live in free-market societies, so investment takes place according to the laws of the market. All that money and investment is flowing into AI because it is simply the most profitable use of resources. And when society maximizes profits, it maximizes efficiency — ensuring that, on aggregate, everyone is better off over the long run.

There are a lot of problems with this story. First, we do not live in free-market societies. We live in capitalist societies — that is, societies dominated by capital. Capital is not distributed into lots of little businesses each producing widgets in perfect competition with one another. Capital agglomerates until it is concentrated within a few massive, monopolistic corporations, controlled by a few powerful men.

These massive corporations can afford to ignore what’s profitable in the short run pursuit of what will bring their owners immense wealth and power in the long run. Just take Amazon. It was unprofitable for years while Jeff Bezos channeled more and more money into expansion. Investors continued to funnel billions into Amazon’s coffers because they were betting that Bezos could carve out a powerful monopoly. And they were right. Corporate concentration and monopoly power trump competition and efficiency every time.

Despite all the hype about AI, LLMs are not currently profitable. OpenAI and Anthropic — the two companies whose fate is tied entirely to the performance of their LLMs — have yet to make a profit. And yet both companies are trying to list on the stock market chasing valuations of $1 trillion.

Why? Because these two companies have successfully enclosed — that is, taken and put walls around — vast areas of human knowledge. Now they are selling it back to us in the form of strange, sycophantic chatbots that put all this knowledge back together in unpredictable — and sometimes completely useless — ways. Still, investors are betting that this innovation will revolutionize capitalist production, and that one or both of these companies will continue to hold immense power over the market.

All the other companies in the ecosystem — the ones building the infrastructure, the ones producing the chips, the ones powering the data centers — are dependent upon the performance of the LLMs at the center of the boom. Which is why companies like Nvidia and Oracle are locked into a circular network of financing with OpenAI — they’re funding OpenAI while it loses money, because their profits are contingent upon the company’s success.

This is where the next correction to our original story comes in. Right now, we are absolutely in a bubble when it comes to AI. That doesn’t mean the technology won’t permanently change the way our economy works — but it does mean that the tech won’t be as profitable as most investors are expecting, especially over the short term. In other words, not only are our markets not free — they’re not efficient either.

Investors are betting that this tech cycle will be like the last one — the one where companies like Google, Meta, and Amazon enclosed the entire internet. Lots of those companies took a long time to make any profit, because they were investing to eke out a market-dominating position — not to maximize short-term profits. The companies involved in the AI boom are trying to do the same thing, but it’s not working.

First, there’s too much competition among US LLM providers. It’s not just ChatGPT and Claude now — Gemini and Copilot are nipping at their heels. Then there’s competition from China. Chinese companies have already been able to create their own LLMs — they might not be as good as the originals, but it doesn’t matter, because they’re incredibly cheap.

And then, there’s the productivity puzzle. For the LLMs to be profitable over the long run, they need to be rolled out by lots of businesses that won’t cancel their subscriptions as soon as a cheaper option is available — which means the productivity gains of introducing the technology have to be very clear. But not many businesses have seen significant productivity gains from the introduction of the technology. In this context, it’s not clear how all these LLMs are going to generate the profits required to produce a decent return on that $1 trillion investment.

When investors realize that some of the bets they have made aren’t going to yield much of a return, the cash will dry up. The circular webs of financing will collapse. Companies will go under. And the world will be left with hundreds of massive data centers without enough customers. Compute will become extremely cheap — just like accessing the internet did after the telecom companies spent billions competing to lay fiber optic cables in the 1990s.

The boom will get going again after the bust — with valuations returning to more sensible levels. A few of the massive tech companies will buy up the remnants of the others, leaving the market even more concentrated. The technology will become pedestrian as it is incorporated into every area of our lives. People will get real about what AI can do and what it can’t do.

Of course, millions of people will lose their jobs and their savings during the bust. Wealth and power will become even more concentrated, as the largest tech companies buy up their defunct competitors, before leveraging their control over the technological infrastructure that most other businesses require to function. They will use this power to further capture our democracies, lobbying politicians to wage war on their foreign competition.

Our environment will also be permanently changed. Erald Kolasi and Jesse Damiani have just written an excellent piece calculating the environmental impact of the AI boom. They estimate that, in 2026, AI will be responsible for 1.1 percent of total global energy demand. AI is already using more energy than the whole of the United Kingdom. Meanwhile, many communities are being forced to go without water, while others experience striking “heat island” effects from the astonishing amounts of heat being pumped out by these megaliths.

After years of hype and trillions of dollars, the AI boom will leave us with a captured economy, a corrupted democracy, and a devastated environment. We’ll be told that this is just how markets work — sometimes they go up, sometimes they go down. But this narrative obscures how decisions are really made in capitalist economies.

As I showed in my book, Vulture Capitalism, capitalist economies are characterized by pervasive central planning. Monopolistic corporations work with corrupt politicians to decide who gets what, while using “the market” as a veil to conceal their power. The AI boom is no different. A few powerful capitalists decided that we would spend several years devoting all our time and money toward the development and roll out of AI — and so we did.

“The market” didn’t decide that AI would be our future. Capital did. And when the devastating consequences of their decisions become clear, we cannot allow them to hide behind disembodied market forces. Capital took us down this route, and capital must be made to pay. The politicians aren’t going to go after their wealthy backers; that part is on us. So block new data centers, strip them for parts, and start organizing your communities and your workplaces for the fightback.

title: Dems select their candidate to face longtime GOP lawmaker who balked at Virginia redistricting
description: A crowded seven-candidate Democratic primary in Virginia's 1st Congressional District sets up a November showdown against Rep. Rob Wittman.
fullText:
Shannon Taylor won the Democratic primary Tuesday in Virginia's 1st Congressional District.

The victory sets up a Nov. 3 showdown between the Democrat nominee and longtime Republican Rep. Rob Wittman, who has been in Congress since 2007.

Although Republicans have long held the seat, Democrats hope that shifting suburban voting patterns around the blue enclave of Richmond will make the district more competitive for them.

2026 Midterms: Primaries, Key Races And Election Results

Democrats in Virginia sought to redraw the congressional map this year. If adopted, Virginia's 1st Congressional District, and many others, would be significantly more favorable to Democrats. The map was ultimately struck down and is not being used in this year's election, relieving pressure of Wittman's seat being at risk.

The district remains "lean Republican," according to the Cook Political Report.

The Democratic primary to face Wittman in the fall featured a crowded seven-candidate field.

The candidates included Henrico Commonwealth's Attorney Shannon Taylor, former Justice Department official Salaam Bhatti, Army veteran Jason Knapp, attorney Mel Tull, environmental advocate Tim Cywinski, attorney Ericka Kopp and educator Elizabeth Beggs.

Democrats are targeting the district as part of their broader effort to flip control of the House, though the district spans Richmond's outer suburbs, Williamsburg and Virginia's Chesapeake Bay region and has traditionally favored Republicans.

Wittman has represented the district since 2007 and is seeking another term.

Virginia's congressional primaries were held in August rather than the state's traditional June schedule after litigation over new congressional maps delayed the nomination process.

title: US suspends avocado inspections in Mexican state of Michoacan due to threat
description: The United States announced Wednesday that it had suspended all government operations in the Mexican state of Michoacan because of a "threat to U.S. interests," including a halt to the inspections of ...
fullText:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — The United States announced Wednesday that it had suspended all government operations in the Mexican state of Michoacan because of a "threat to U.S. interests," including a halt to the inspections of avocados required for their export.

While the U.S. Embassy did not specify the nature of the threat in its security alert, Michoacan Gov. Alfredo Ramírez Bedolla said on social media that the temporary halt to inspections was intended to safeguard workers following recent arrests linked to extortion. The inspections are necessary for avocados to be shipped to the United States and their suspension could disrupt exports.

The western state of Michoacan is the leading exporter of avocados to the U.S. and has a high level of organized crime activity with at least four cartels — designated as terrorist organizations by the Trump administration — operating in the region. Besides trafficking drugs, cartels also make money through extortion, including of the avocado industry.

Michoacan State Security Secretary Antonio Cruz told The Associated Press that one of the arrests mentioned by the governor was of "El Poncho," the alias of Alfonso Fernández Magallón, leader of a local cartel operating in the avocado-growing region around Los Reyes.

U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson welcomed the arrest, which came over the weekend. The U.S. government had offered a $5 million reward for Fernández Magallón's arrest.

Cruz said his department was unaware of any direct incidents involving the avocado inspectors. Nevertheless, 300 security personnel were deployed to the Los Reyes area as a preventive measure.

The governor said the priority was to "ensure the security conditions necessary for these operations to resume normally," as has happened in the past.

Mexico supplies approximately 80% of U.S. avocado imports - a product known in the region as "green gold." Its cultivation generates around 200,000 jobs in Michoacán alone.

In 2025, Mexico sold $3.65 billion worth of avocados to the United States, and in the first four months of this year, those exports rose by 35% compared to the same period in the previous year.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture sends inspectors in Mexico to monitor plantations and packing houses to ensure that exported produce is free of pests. Threats and violence against the inspectors have caused the U.S. to suspend inspections in the past.

title: De Blasio: Talarico’s ‘kitchen table’ talk ‘worst nightmare for Republicans’
description: Former New York Mayor Bill de Blasio (D) said Tuesday that Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico’s discussion of “kitchen table issues” is Republicans’ “worst nightmare” as Democrats look t...
fullText:
Former New York Mayor Bill de Blasio (D) said Tuesday that Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico's discussion of "kitchen table issues" is Republicans' "worst nightmare" as Democrats look to clinch a Senate seat in the Lone Star State.

"When you listen to Talarico, he is going after billionaires. He's saying they're not paying their fair share of taxes. He is talking about commonsense kitchen table issues, which his opponent isn't," de Blasio told Fox News's Sean Hannity.

"This is the worst nightmare for Republicans that Democrats actually get their act together and talk about the kitchen table," he added.

Many 2026 midterm Democratic campaigns have focused on the idea of affordability for constituents, including Talarico's.

According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published this week, Democrats had a small lead over Republicans when it came to economic messaging for the first time in close to 10 years.

Talarico states on his website, that "the biggest divide in this country is not left vs. right," adding the largest split is "top vs. bottom."

"Billionaires want us looking left and right at each other instead of looking up at them," Talarico added. "The people at the top work so hard to keep us angry and divided because our unity is a threat to their wealth and power."

The GOP is facing rocky midterm terrain when it comes to the economy, with Americans expressing economic concerns in recent polling and increased gas prices due to the war in Iran.

According to AAA, the average price of a gallon of gas as of Wednesday afternoon was about $4.08, up from about $3.16 last year.

title: Washington man charged with killing bald eagle
description: A Washington man faces federal charges after allegedly shooting and killing a bald eagle near his property.
fullText:
Someone heard a gunshot, and before long, U.S. Department of Fish and Wildlife officers had been dispatched to the rural community of Brush Prairie, Washington, where they found a dead bald eagle, the ground around its head stained red with blood.

On Tuesday, a 66-year-old Clark County man was charged with shooting and killing the bird with a shotgun in violation of federal law, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Washington.

Benjamin G. Allen is accused of violating the Bald and Gold Eagle Protection Act and unlawfully killing a migratory bird, both misdemeanors.

The incident took place on February 5, 2026. A veterinary exam revealed the eagle had two shotgun pellets in its brain, the U.S. Attorney's Office said.

Allen, who according to investigators kept chickens not far from where the dead eagle was discovered, is scheduled to appear in U.S. District Court in early September.

He could face up to a year in prison and a $500,000 fine for the first charge and up to six months and a $5,000 fine for the second.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife investigated the case.

Eagles are effective hunters, equipped with superior eyesight and powerful talons, and while they prefer fish and carrion, they'll target free-ranging chickens if given the chance, according to BackYardChickens.com.

Millions of fans have been following the saga of Jackie, a bald eagle who earned fame by appearing on Big Bear Valley's Big Bear Eagle Nest Cam but who has been recovering at a California raptor center after a July 17 altercation with two juvenile eagles.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Washington man charged with killing bald eagle

title: Texas judge rules that law regulating firearm suppressors and some guns can't be enforced
description: A federal judge in Texas on Wednesday struck down a 1930s law that imposed regulations on firearm suppressors and guns that are considered the most dangerous, more than a year after President Donald T...
fullText:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A federal judge in Texas on Wednesday struck down a 1930s law that imposed regulations on firearm suppressors and guns that are considered the most dangerous, more than a year after President Donald Trump signed a bill eliminating taxes on those items.

The ruling could allow firearm owners to purchase firearm suppressors — known as silencers — short-barreled rifles, short-barreled shotguns and other certain firearms without registration, while also removing a layer of background checks. Last year, Republicans eliminated a $200 tax on those devices under Trump's massive tax and spending cut bill.

The regulations are required under the National Firearms Act, passed in the 1930s in response to concerns about mafia violence. Groups that support gun restrictions said the law still has important safety protections and criticized the ruling as reckless.

U.S. District Judge James Hendrix said because there were no longer taxes under the act, the regulation should not continue either.

"No longer can the challenged NFA provisions be justified — as they have been for nearly 90 years — under Congress's taxing power," Hendrix wrote.

The U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, which enforces the regulations, did not immediately return an email seeking comment.

The National Firearms Act has been in effect since 1934 and establishes key differences and regulates firearms considered the most dangerous. Because the act implemented a tax on the item, the registration was often used to ensure the tax was paid, gun rights groups said.

The ruling was a major victory for gun rights groups who said they hoped the decision would create momentum to ultimately send the case to the U.S. Supreme Court.

"This ruling will set a precedent we can now argue in courts across the country to allow Americans to exercise their Second Amendment rights without fear of being placed on some government registry," the Second Amendment Foundation said in a statement.

While background checks will still be required under federal law, Giffords Law Center Chief Counsel Adam Skaggs said the registration process included notifying local law enforcement and asking if there was any reason to deny the application.

"That process effectively functioned as a heightened background check for NFA weapons, and that process is no longer enforceable," Skaggs said in a statement.

In June, the number of registered firearm suppressors in the U.S. was more than 6.4 million, according to the ATF.

"Today's ruling is a dangerous step backward for public safety," the Giffords Law Center, which advocates for tougher gun control measures, said in a statement.

Wilder is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Trump files emergency motion to block BBC from getting financial details about business empire
description: President Trump’s attorney filed an emergency motion Wednesday seeking to block the BBC from obtaining financial records linked to his trust. The British broadcaster received approval from a judge lat...
fullText:
President Trump's attorney filed an emergency motion Wednesday seeking to block the BBC from obtaining financial records linked to his trust.

The British broadcaster received approval from a judge late last month to probe the president's financial documents after Trump claimed he experienced losses due to an episode of the company's "Panorama" series titled "Trump: A Second Chance?"

In the footage, the BBC strung together three separate portions of a speech from Trump to make it look as if he encouraged a violent attack on the Capitol.

"The BBC's improperly broad subpoena demands the Trust's confidential tax, ownership, and financial records for approximately 400 entities," Trump's attorney Alejandro Brito wrote in the legal filing.

"Once the Trust were to begin handing those records over to the BBC, that disclosure could not be undone, and the Trust's pending objections could not restore what the BBC will already have seen," Brito added.

If the emergency motion is not approved, the BBC would be granted insight on Trump's crypto and stock profit, as well as business transactions from at least 400 entities and companies tied to his personal assets managed by family.

Last month, Judge Enjoliqué Aytch Lett granted the BBC's subpoena to review documents from the Donald J. Trump Revocable Trust dating to Jan. 1, 2023.

Her approval requires that the trust start producing documents by Thursday.

"Against the Trust's irreversible injury, the BBC cannot point to any injury, only to brief delay, which does not constitute harm. Fact discovery remains open for months, and the BBC has never explained why it needed a non-party's complete financial records within ten days or how a short stay would impair its defense," Brito wrote.

The BBC has apologized for the documentary edit but has strongly rebuked Trump's push for a payout and attempted to dismiss the lawsuit against the company, arguing U.S. courts hold no legal jurisdiction over the foreign corporation.

The president has refused to back down and recently requested that District Judge Roy Altman allow him to alter the lawsuit in a manner that would shield his financial documents from being reviewed by the British broadcaster.

title: Israeli President Herzog calls antisemitism a 'contamination of societies' as hate crimes surge
description: NYPD data shows anti-Jewish incidents account for 56.9% of all hate crimes in 2026 as Israeli President Isaac Herzog warns antisemitism is a global contamination.
fullText:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog issued a stern warning about the global spread of antisemitism in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital at his Jerusalem residence.

"Antisemitism is an age-old plague which should be dealt with by everybody, by all societies. It's not an Israeli issue or only a Jewish issue," he said.

"It's a contamination of societies that starts with the Jews — never ends with them. It's the most dangerous phenomena that has to be dealt with aggressively, with no mercy, with full adjudication, and most importantly, with education," he added.

Exclusive: Israeli President Herzog Blasts Mamdani, Praises Trump, Sounds Alarm On Iran

Herzog's warning comes as newly released New York City Police Department (NYPD) data show anti-Jewish incidents accounted for 56.9% of all confirmed hate crimes since the start of 2026, even though Jewish New Yorkers make up only about 10% of the city's population.

Herzog pointed to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whom he accused of spreading hate and compromising the lives of New Yorkers.

"Mamdani does not respect my nation's right for self-determination — the Jewish people's inherent right to have a nation of their own. And he's basically spreading blasphemy, hate, antisemitic rhetoric. He should understand that he's risking his own citizens, he's risking their safety, well-being and life," Herzog told Fox News Digital.

In a video posted on social media on July 21, Mamdani called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "a war criminal" and "the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people."

Days later, Raul Morales, 51, allegedly yelled "Allahu Akbar" while stabbing two men on Manhattan's Upper West Side, including one who was visibly identifiable as Jewish.

Suspect Arrested After Allegedly Yelling 'Allahu Akbar,' Stabbing 2 Men In Nyc Attack

"We've seen the stabbing just a few days ago... just because somebody was dressed as an Orthodox Jew. This cannot be accepted in New York, which is a city that is dear to our heart, dear to Israelis, and dear to me personally," Herzog said.

More broadly, a report released last month by the J7 Large Communities' Task Force Against Antisemitism found that 20 people were killed in antisemitic attacks across seven countries outside Israel in 2025, marking the deadliest year for such violence in the Jewish diaspora since 1994.

The J7 comprises Jewish communities in the United States, Australia, Canada, Argentina, the United Kingdom, Germany and France.

According to the report, more than 23,000 antisemitic incidents were recorded across the J7 countries last year, representing a 97% increase in violent attacks and a 136% rise in overall incidents compared with 2022.

"Of course, Israel is doing its best, but it has to be an effort with governments all over the world, law enforcement agencies, educational systems and Jewish communities, which we care about a lot," Herzog said, in reference to confronting Jew-hatred.

Referencing a recent article by professor Niall Ferguson titled "The Death of History," he said, "How much TikTok or the social networks distort the facts of history? They negate the worst and greatest horror of humankind, the Holocaust. And that's why we have to stand up together and combat it," he told Fox News Digital.

Herzog stressed that misinformation spread through distorted and superficial channels makes it easy to smear Israel on social media, but that such narratives do not reflect reality.

German Officials Warn Islamist, Far-left Rhetoric Driving Spike In Antisemitic Attacks

"[Israel] is the place where the Startup Nation flourishes. This is the place where great ideas are given to the world and contribute enormously to the world in so many great fields, from health to energy, to science, to agriculture, to food security, to what not. There's a reason why Americans who visit our country, young Americans, fall in love with this country," he said.

Growing antisemitism, coupled with polarization within and between Jewish communities and a weakening sense of Jewish identity in some places, led Herzog to launch Voice of the People in April 2023. The initiative brings together a council of 150 emerging leaders — one-third from Israel, one-third from the United States and the remainder from around the world.

Leaders are selected through an algorithm from thousands of candidates and serve rotating terms of roughly two years, developing ideas to address challenges facing the Jewish world.

The initiative held an in-person kickoff summit in March 2025 in Haifa, featuring Herzog and bringing together all council members, reflecting his belief in building the next generation of Jewish leadership, which he described as one of his main tasks.

"I'm overjoyed by the great ideas I see and feel, and I hope that around November we will have a new registration starting for the next slot, the next cohort, and I invite as many Jewish friends to register," he said.

description: Will you get today's player in as few attempts as possible?
fullText:

title: 'Show me they want me' - will World Cup hero Torres stay at Barcelona?
description: Ferran Torres has come under fire from Barcelona supporters after leaving the door open to a potential move away from the club.
fullText:
Ferran Torres will return to Barcelona later this month having cemented his name in the country's football folklore following his extra-time winner to seal Spain's second World Cup triumph.

His profile and marketability has significantly grown and those around him will be keen to ensure he makes the most of a career-defining moment.

But a summer dominated by World Cup celebrations has given way to transfer speculation, fuelled by the forward's own comments during a media tour in the United States.

The 26-year-old is under contract with Barcelona until June 2027 meaning, if he does not reach an agreement with the Catalan giants, Torres will be able to negotiate with another club as a free agent from January.

So, as Barcelona's players gradually report back for pre-season, does Spain's World Cup hero's future remain at the Nou Camp?

The uncertainty surrounding Torres' future has intensified following a series of high-profile television appearances in the United States for a promotional tour with his sportswear sponsor.

Asked where he expected to be playing next season, Torres replied: "I have a contract with Barcelona but, in football, you never know.

"We are waiting to make the right decision. Right now, all I know is that I have to be in training for Barcelona on 12 August. Let's see what happens."

Asked what Barcelona need to do to keep him, he said: "Show me they want me, come to negotiate."

Reflecting on his winner against Argentina in the World Cup final, he added: "I've watched it thousands of times. When I finished the game, I didn't remember the goal. It was unbelievable. I can't describe it with words."

The speculation only increased when he was asked directly about reported interest from Paris St-Germain.

"Every time these teams want you it's a good thing," Torres said. "You never know because in football everything can change in one minute, so I have to be ready for everything."

Asked how he would approach such a career-defining decision, Torres replied: "Trying to think what is going to make me happiest."

Torres' comments have frustrated many Barcelona supporters, who believe he has been too open about the possibility of leaving the club and attempting to strengthen his negotiating position.

Fans have also taken issue with what they see as his carefully chosen wording when discussing interest from other teams, particularly given that he has never established himself as a regular starter or consistently lived up to expectations since joining Barcelona from Manchester City in 2022.

Barcelona remain relaxed about Torres' situation despite the growing uncertainty surrounding his future. They say they will speak to him when he returns to training, as planned.

He was not a regular starter under Hansi Flick last season and ended the campaign with 21 goals and three assists in 49 appearances.

But he is one of the club's most trusted and versatile attacking options, rotating primarily with Robert Lewandowski - who has since signed for Chicago Fire - as a central striker while also providing cover across the front three.

Barcelona are ultimately keen to extend his contract but any new agreement is expected to keep Torres within the existing wage structure rather than include a substantial salary increase.

Reports suggest the club would look to delay formal negotiations until September - after the transfer window has closed - so as not to affect Financial Fair Play calculations and their ability to do business during the current window.

Renewing Torres' deal would also reportedly trigger, external a payment of almost £7m to former club Manchester City, because of a clause included in his contract when he signed in the 2022 January transfer window.

Barcelona have received no formal offers for the Spain international although, as with any member of the squad, they would consider an offer if one were made.

PSG, managed by former Barcelona coach Luis Enrique, remain interested in the forward and are monitoring developments closely as Barcelona prepare to present their proposal.

The forward may feel he heads into those negotiations from a position of strength.

They come with the club still seeking a long-term number nine solution, with a move for Atletico Madrid's Julian Alvarez remaining uncertain.

That means, following Lewandowski's departure at the end of his contract in June, Torres is the only senior Barcelona forward with significant experience of playing as a central striker.
